Requirement: Features of Gemini Enterprise for CX that are Non-GA or Pre-GA **MUST NOT** be used.
Rationale: Any capability not designated GA is governed by Google's Pre-GA Offerings Terms in the Service Specific Terms. Those terms state that pre-GA offerings are provided as is with limited or no support, may be changed or discontinued without notice, carry no production SLA, and are not necessarily covered by the compliance certifications (HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO 27001, FedRAMP) that the organization's assurance posture depends on. A Pre-GA capability handling member conversation content therefore sits outside the contractual perimeter the BAA establishes.
Notes: GA status is determined only from the vendor's release notes and product documentation with the Pre-GA Offerings Terms disclaimer removed. Console availability, marketing pages, partner training material, and press announcements are not authoritative. Gemini Enterprise for CX spans four documentation trees with independent release cadences, so GA status is confirmed per component and per feature rather than for the suite. Re-verify at every release-note review cycle.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-7 (Least Functionality), SA-4 (Acquisition Process)

Requirement: Commerce agents **MUST NOT** be deployed.
Rationale: Google's own documentation states that Commerce agents are not yet released, describing them only as coming soon. An unreleased product has no published security documentation, no encryption or residency configuration surface, no IAM model, and no entry in the HIPAA covered products list. The intended capability set compounds this: Google describes Commerce agents as executing consented actions on a customer's behalf, which is a write-capable autonomous surface reaching commerce and order systems.
Notes: This prohibition is a specific application of this guide's baseline prohibition on Non-GA and Pre-GA features, and stands until Commerce agents reach GA, appear in the HIPAA covered products list, and are assessed under a fresh capability certification. Track the product page and the CX Agent Studio release notes for the transition. Nothing in this guide anticipates the control surface Commerce agents will present.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: The `v1beta` CX Agent Studio API and the `v1alpha1` CX Insights API **MUST NOT** be called from production workloads.
Rationale: Both product APIs publish a pre-release version alongside the stable one, and the pre-release surface carries the Pre-GA Offerings Terms rather than the production terms. A client library or integration pinned to v1beta or v1alpha1 silently places production conversation traffic outside the supported and compliance-covered API surface, and the version is a substring of an endpoint path that no console screen displays.
Notes: Audit deployed client configuration, not console settings: the version appears in the endpoint path and in generated client stubs. CX Agent Studio audit log entries record the API version in the method name, for example google.cloud.ces.v1beta.EvaluationService.RunEvaluation, so a Cloud Logging query for method names containing v1beta or v1alpha1 is the detective control. Some evaluation operations are only offered on v1beta - restrict those to non-production projects rather than promoting the version.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles)

Requirement: The Google Maps tool in CX Agent Studio **MUST NOT** be enabled on any agent application.
Rationale: The tools overview flags the Google Maps tool as Preview while presenting it in the same tool picker as generally available tool types. A builder selecting it from that list receives no signal that the resulting agent has left the supported configuration, and the tool sends conversation-derived location context to a mapping surface outside the guide's assessed boundary.
Notes: This is a specific application of this guide's baseline prohibition on Non-GA and Pre-GA features, restated because the console does not segregate Preview tools from GA tools in the picker. Enforce by tool-type review during agent approval rather than by expecting builders to notice the marker. Every other tool type on the overview page was GA at the time of authoring; re-check the page at each review because the picker composition changes without a release note.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SA-4 (Acquisition Process)

Requirement: CX Insights capabilities documented as Preview, including fine-grained access control, conversation datasets, and multiple scorecards, **MUST NOT** be used as the control of record or as a production dependency.
Rationale: The CX Insights release notes place several capabilities in Preview, and one of them - fine-grained access control - is the only mechanism the product offers for scoping an analyst to a subset of conversations. Building an access model on a Pre-GA feature means the boundary protecting member conversation content is one that Google may change or withdraw without notice and does not warrant under the compliance terms.
Notes: The practical consequence is carried by the CX Insights access requirement in this guide: because fine-grained access control cannot be the control of record, project-level CX Insights access must be compensated by a deliberately small approved group plus Data Access audit logging. Do not read this requirement as prohibiting evaluation of authorized views in a non-production project - it prohibits depending on them for a production access decision.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management), 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CM-7 (Least Functionality), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: A capability certification review **MUST** be completed and approved before any Gemini Enterprise for CX component processes production member conversation data.
Rationale: Every component of this suite reads or writes unstructured member conversation, which is among the densest concentrations of protected health information the organization holds, and several of its configuration decisions cannot be reversed after first use. Certification is the gate that forces the irreversible decisions - encryption specification, residency region, project boundary, perimeter membership, retention - to be made deliberately rather than discovered after data has landed.
Notes: Sequence the certification before the first agent application, the first CX Insights location initialization, and the first conversation ingestion. The CX Insights encryption specification, the CX Agent Studio CMEK integration, the residency region, and the conversation TTL each close permanently at or before first use, so a certification that runs after a pilot has ingested real conversations cannot remediate them without deleting and rebuilding the resources.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (Risk Analysis), 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CA-2 (Control Assessments), RA-3 (Risk Assessment), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures); NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1): GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE

Requirement: Newly released Gemini Enterprise for CX features **MUST** be reviewed and explicitly approved before enablement, on a review cadence no longer than monthly.
Rationale: The suite ships features continuously across four independent release-note streams, and the CX Agent Studio notes alone record ten capability additions in the eleven months following general availability. Features arrive enabled and visible in the console rather than behind an opt-in, so an unreviewed release becomes a production configuration change that no one authorized. Agents as tools and traffic splitting are both examples of additions that materially changed the authorization and rollout surface.
Notes: Assign a named owner for each of the four release-note streams: CX Agent Studio, CX Insights, Agent Assist, and the suite root. The review asks three questions per entry - does it change what data leaves the boundary, does it change what identity an action runs as, and does it change a setting this guide pins. Record the review outcome so the certification evidence stays current between annual reassessments.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-4 (Impact Analyses), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

Requirement: The configuration baseline for every Gemini Enterprise for CX project - guardrails, tools, deployment channels, encryption, residency, retention, and audit settings - **MUST** be documented and drift-checked at least quarterly.
Rationale: Almost every control in this guide is a project or agent setting that a holder of the relevant editor role can change without a deployment, a code review, or a change ticket. The ten-role IAM family means several different people can each alter one facet of the security posture independently, so the aggregate configuration is nobody's job to know unless a baseline records what it is supposed to be.
Notes: Capture the baseline as configuration exported through the API rather than as console screenshots, so the comparison can be automated. The high-value drift signals are guardrail level changes, new tool registrations, a deployment channel gaining public access, and a change to security settings - all four appear in Admin Activity or Data Access audit logs and can be alerted on directly.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

Requirement: Personnel who build, deploy, or administer Gemini Enterprise for CX agent applications **SHOULD** complete role-specific training covering the confused-deputy tool execution model and the irreversible configuration decisions documented in this guide.
Rationale: The two failure modes most likely to produce a material incident in this product are both invisible in the builder's workflow: a tool executes with the service agent's permissions rather than the caller's, and several encryption and residency settings cannot be changed after first use. Neither is surfaced by the console at the moment the decision is made, so a builder who has not been told will not infer them from the interface.
Notes: The training does not need to be lengthy. It needs to convey four things: tools run as the platform identity, retrieval is not permission-aware, the project boundary is the real security boundary, and CMEK and residency close at first use. The source material is the tool execution model, the data store retrieval model, the CX Insights encryption specification, the CX Agent Studio CMEK integration, and the residency region.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(5) (Security Awareness and Training); NIST 800-53: AT-2 (Literacy Training and Awareness), AT-3 (Role-based Training), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles)

Requirement: Administrative and builder access to CX Agent Studio, CX Insights, and Agent Assist **MUST** be federated through the organization's enterprise identity provider.
Rationale: Federation is the trust anchor that extends existing conditional access policy, multi-factor enforcement, joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle, and session control to this suite. Without it, access to a surface holding member conversation content depends on a separate identity store whose deprovisioning is not tied to the HR record, leaving orphaned accounts with standing access to conversation transcripts after a person leaves.
Notes: Federate the Google Cloud identity used to reach the console and the APIs, not just the console. Confirm that the API path is covered as well, because a service account key or a personal gcloud credential bypasses federation entirely, which is why this guide separately prohibits service account keys for these roles.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication), 164.308(a)(3) (Workforce Security); NIST 800-53: IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)), IA-5 (Authenticator Management), IA-8 (Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users)), AC-17 (Remote Access)

Requirement: Multi-factor authentication **MUST** be enforced for every account holding any `ces.googleapis.com` or `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com` role.
Rationale: A single compromised builder credential is sufficient to register a tool that reaches a backend system, to change a guardrail level, or to read conversation transcripts in bulk, because these roles operate on a surface that has no second approval step. Credential theft through phishing or reuse is the dominant initial access vector, and MFA is the control that breaks it.
Notes: Enforce at the identity provider so the requirement covers console, gcloud, and API access uniformly. Phishing-resistant factors are preferred for the admin, securitySettingsEditor, and deploymentEditor roles, which are the three that can change the security posture or push to production.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication); NIST 800-53: IA-2(1) (Multi-factor Authentication to Privileged Accounts), IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)), IA-5 (Authenticator Management)

Requirement: The `ces.googleapis.com/admin` role **MUST** be granted only to named individual administrators.
Rationale: The admin role provides full access to CX Agent Studio resources, which means it collapses the ten-role separation the product otherwise offers into a single grant covering apps, agents, tools, guardrails, evaluations, security settings, and deployments. A group grant makes the effective administrator population a function of group membership managed elsewhere, so the number of people who can silently alter the security posture is unknown to the people accountable for it.
Notes: Google publishes ten CX Agent Studio roles precisely so that admin does not have to be the default. Grant appEditor, agentEditor, toolsEditor, guardrailsEditor, evalsEditor, securitySettingsEditor, or deploymentEditor to match the actual job. Reserve admin for a small named set and include it in the quarterly entitlement recertification. Group grants are prohibited under this requirement: a group makes the effective administrator population a function of membership managed elsewhere.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management); NIST 800-53: AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-6(1) (Authorize Access to Security Functions), AC-2 (Account Management), AC-3 (Access Enforcement)

Requirement: Basic IAM roles - Owner, Editor, and Viewer - **MUST NOT** be granted on any project hosting a Gemini Enterprise for CX component.
Rationale: Basic roles predate the product's own role family and grant permissions across every API enabled in the project, including `ces.googleapis.com` and `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com`. A project Viewer therefore reads conversation content, and a project Editor registers tools and changes guardrails, without either grant appearing in any CX-specific access review. Basic roles also expand automatically as Google adds APIs and permissions.
Notes: Audit existing bindings before enabling the APIs, because a pre-existing project Editor binding becomes a CX Agent Studio editor binding the moment the API is turned on. This is one of the reasons this guide requires a dedicated project per trust domain rather than reuse of an existing one.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-2 (Account Management)

Requirement: The `ces.googleapis.com/securitySettingsEditor` role **MUST** be held by a different set of individuals than those holding `ces.googleapis.com/agentEditor` or `ces.googleapis.com/toolsEditor`.
Rationale: Security settings govern redaction, retention, and export configuration, while agent and tool editors govern what the agent does and what it can reach. Where one person holds both, the same identity can register a tool that reaches sensitive data and relax the redaction that would have caught the disclosure, with no second party in the path. The product's role split makes this separation available at no operational cost.
Notes: This is a separation-of-duties control, not a least-privilege control - it constrains combinations rather than individual grants. Implement it as a check in the access-request workflow and as a periodic query over IAM policy bindings, because IAM itself will not prevent the combination.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(3) (Workforce Security), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: AC-5 (Separation of Duties), AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-6(1) (Authorize Access to Security Functions)

Requirement: The `ces.googleapis.com/deploymentEditor` role **MUST** be restricted to personnel explicitly authorized to promote changes to production.
Rationale: Deployment is the only step between an agent configuration and live member traffic. Because the product supports traffic splitting across deployment environments, a deployment editor can also redirect a share of production conversations to a different agent version without changing the agent itself, which is a production change that leaves no trace in the agent's own changelog.
Notes: This pairs with the traffic-splitting control elsewhere in this guide, which prohibits directing production traffic to an unreviewed agent version. Deployment actions appear in Admin Activity audit logs and should be alerted on. Agent builders do not receive this role by default; where a builder also promotes, the grant is a named exception with a recorded approver.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(3) (Workforce Security); NIST 800-53: AC-5 (Separation of Duties), AC-6 (Least Privilege), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-5 (Access Restrictions for Change)

Requirement: The `ces.googleapis.com/client` role **MUST** be granted only to the service identities used by approved deployment channels.
Rationale: The client role provides query access to agents, which is the runtime conversation path rather than an administrative one. It is the role a token broker's service account holds, so every grant of it is effectively a new channel through which conversations can be initiated. Granting it to a group makes the set of parties who can converse with a production agent, and therefore reach whatever its tools reach, unbounded.
Notes: Inventory client role holders alongside the approved deployment channel inventory - the two lists should match exactly. A client grant with no corresponding approved channel is either an undocumented integration or a leftover from testing. Human users and broad groups are never appropriate holders of this role, because it is the runtime conversation path rather than an administrative one.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication), AC-2 (Account Management)

Requirement: The CX Agent Studio service agent `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-ces.iam.gserviceaccount.com` **MUST** be granted only the minimum IAM roles required by the approved tools in that project.
Rationale: Google documents that OpenAPI tool actions execute with the permissions granted to the CX Agent Studio service account rather than those of the end user, and names minimum IAM on that account as one of its three recommended mitigations. Every role granted to the service agent is therefore added to the effective reach of every agent in the project, including agents a different team built and agents reachable by anonymous callers.
Notes: Treat each new grant to this service agent as a change to the blast radius of every agent in the project, and require the same review as adding a tool. Where a tool needs broad access to a backend, the correct answer is usually a separate project rather than a broader grant. Google's other two stated mitigations, dedicated projects and VPC Service Controls, are each carried by their own requirement in this guide.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management); NIST 800-53: AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication), CM-7 (Least Functionality); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API5 (Broken Function Level Authorization); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI03 (Identity and Privilege Abuse)

Requirement: Service account keys **MUST NOT** be created for any identity holding a Gemini Enterprise for CX role.
Rationale: A downloaded service account key is a long-lived bearer credential that bypasses federation, conditional access, and multi-factor enforcement, and it does not expire on personnel departure. Because the client role is a conversation-initiation credential and the editor roles alter what agents can reach, a leaked key for either is directly equivalent to unauthorized access to member conversation content.
Notes: Use workload identity federation for external callers and attached service accounts for workloads inside Google Cloud. The self-hosted token broker pattern runs on Cloud Run with an attached service account and needs no key. Enforce with the organization policy constraint that disables service account key creation.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication); NIST 800-53: IA-5 (Authenticator Management), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication), AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Requirement: Entitlements to all `ces.googleapis.com` and `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com` roles **MUST** be recertified at least quarterly by the accountable business owner.
Rationale: Access to this suite accumulates through pilots, incident response, and vendor-led enablement sessions, and none of those paths has a natural expiry. Because CX Insights project-level roles expose every conversation in the project, fine-grained scoping being Pre-GA and therefore unavailable as the control of record, an unreviewed viewer grant is standing access to the complete member conversation corpus rather than to a bounded slice of it.
Notes: Recertify the CX Insights viewer and editor populations with particular care, and treat the approved CX Insights access group as the authoritative list. Recertification should confirm both that the person still needs access and that the role held is still the narrowest one that fits the job.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(3) (Workforce Security), 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management); NIST 800-53: AC-6(7) (Review of User Privileges), AC-2 (Account Management), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Requirement: Contact centre representatives receiving Agent Assist suggestions **MUST** authenticate through the organization's identity provider.
Rationale: Agent Assist places generated summaries, suggested replies, and knowledge excerpts in front of a human handling a live member interaction, and CX Insights subsequently evaluates that human's performance against the same conversation record. Both the disclosure of conversation content to a representative and the attribution of a quality assessment to one depend on knowing reliably which representative was present.
Notes: The agent identifier is also the field CX Insights authorized views filter on, so a reliable representative identity is a prerequisite for any future adoption of fine-grained access control once it leaves Preview. Confirm the identifier propagated by the contact centre platform is the enterprise identity and not a platform-local seat number. The authenticated identity must also be recorded against each conversation the representative handles, since attribution is what makes both the disclosure and any later quality assessment defensible.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication), 164.312(b) (Audit Controls); NIST 800-53: IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)), AU-3 (Content of Audit Records), AC-3 (Access Enforcement)

Requirement: Standing administrative access to production Gemini Enterprise for CX projects **SHOULD** be replaced by time-bound, approved elevation.
Rationale: The administrative actions this suite requires - changing a guardrail, registering a tool, altering retention - are infrequent and individually short. Standing admin rights convert an occasional need into a permanent exposure, and because several of those actions are irreversible in effect, an attacker holding a compromised standing credential does not need to wait for an opportunity.
Notes: Elevation requests should name the change being made so the audit log entry can be correlated to an approval. This pairs with administrative-action alerting: an action with no corresponding elevation record is the signal worth investigating.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management); NIST 800-53: AC-2(11) (Usage Conditions), AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-6(1) (Authorize Access to Security Functions), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), AC-2 (Account Management)

Requirement: Access to Gemini Enterprise for CX administrative surfaces **SHOULD** be conditioned on managed-device posture.
Rationale: Builder and administrator sessions display member conversation content and permit configuration changes that alter what production agents can reach. An unmanaged endpoint provides no assurance of disk encryption, endpoint detection, or absence of credential-stealing malware, so a session from one extends the trust boundary to a device the organization cannot attest.
Notes: Implement at the identity provider or through Context-Aware Access rather than inside the product, which exposes no device-posture control of its own. Apply at minimum to the admin, securitySettingsEditor, deploymentEditor, and CX Insights viewer populations.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.310(b) (Workstation Use); NIST 800-53: AC-17 (Remote Access), IA-3 (Device Identification and Authentication), AC-2(11) (Usage Conditions), AC-2 (Account Management)

Requirement: Guardrails **MUST** be explicitly configured and documented on every agent application rather than left at the shipped default.
Rationale: Google states that each agent application is provided with default guardrails that the builder may modify, but the documentation does not name which safety level or which protections that default comprises. A control whose configured value is unknown cannot be attested to an assessor, cannot be drift-checked, and may change when the vendor revises the default for new applications. Explicit configuration converts an unknown into a baseline.
Notes: Record the four guardrail dimensions per agent: Prompt guard state and outcome, Blocklist contents and match mode, Safety level, and any Rules. This inventory is the artifact the quarterly configuration drift check compares against. Confirm the configured values by reading them back through the API rather than trusting the console form state.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), SI-15 (Information Output Filtering), SI-10 (Information Input Validation); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM01 (Prompt Injection)

Requirement: The Safety guardrail **MUST** be set to Strict or Balanced on every agent application that can reach member data.
Rationale: Google describes Relaxed as prioritizing flexible generation and low latency, which is an explicit trade of harm filtering for responsiveness. On a member-facing health or benefits conversation, the harms the filter addresses are precisely the ones with regulatory and reputational consequence, and latency is not the constraint worth optimizing against them.
Notes: Strict prioritizes deep harm filtering and is the appropriate default for member-facing agents; Balanced is defensible for internal-facing agents where a documented rationale exists. Record which level each agent uses and why, because the choice is invisible in the conversation transcript and cannot be reconstructed later. The Relaxed setting is not acceptable in production on any such agent, because it trades harm filtering for latency.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-15 (Information Output Filtering), SI-10 (Information Input Validation), CM-6 (Configuration Settings); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM09 (Misinformation); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0054 (LLM Jailbreak)

Requirement: The Prompt guard **MUST** be enabled on every agent application, with a defined outcome for a triggered guard.
Rationale: Prompt guard is the product's stated protection against prompt-based attacks such as instructing the agent to ignore its instructions. In this suite the injected instruction does not have to come from the member: tool responses, retrieved data store content, and knowledge base excerpts all enter the model context, so an attacker who can influence any of those sources reaches the same objective indirectly.
Notes: Choosing the outcome matters as much as enabling the guard. An exact response or a handoff to a human is a safe terminal state; a generated response re-enters the model with the adversarial content still in context. Prompt guard is a filter and not a boundary; the architectural half of this control is the separate requirement that tool output and retrieved content be treated as untrusted.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection), SI-15 (Information Output Filtering); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM01 (Prompt Injection); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0051.001 (LLM Prompt Injection - Indirect)

Requirement: A Blocklist guardrail **SHOULD** be configured on member-facing agent applications to suppress terms the organization has designated as prohibited in a generated response.
Rationale: Safety filters address broad harm categories and will not catch organization-specific disclosures: internal system names, unreleased product terms, legally constrained phrasing around coverage determinations, or competitor references. The Blocklist is the only guardrail that encodes organization-specific language, and it applies to agent responses as well as user input.
Notes: Apply the Blocklist to agent responses at minimum; applying it to user input as well is useful for detecting probing but will generate false positives on legitimate member language. The regex match mode is powerful and correspondingly easy to write too broadly - test against a sample of real transcripts before deployment.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-15 (Information Output Filtering), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SI-10 (Information Input Validation); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure)

Requirement: Agent instructions, prompts, application variables, and tool configurations **MUST NOT** contain credentials, API keys, tokens, or connection strings.
Rationale: Agent instructions and application variables are documented as data at rest inside CX Agent Studio and are readable by every holder of the viewer role, exportable through the import and export path, and reachable by the model itself at inference time. A secret placed there is therefore disclosed to a wider population than any secret store would permit and can be surfaced verbatim in a generated response through prompt injection.
Notes: Google supports Secret Manager for OpenAPI tool credentials, and MCP tools carry the same authentication options, so there is a supported path for every case where a secret is genuinely needed. Scan agent instructions and variables for high-entropy strings and known key formats as part of the pre-deployment agent security review.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(i) (Unique User Identification); NIST 800-53: IA-5 (Authenticator Management), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), AC-6 (Least Privilege); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure)

Requirement: Every agent application **MUST** be security reviewed and approved before it is deployed to a channel carrying production traffic.
Rationale: The security posture of an agent is the union of its instructions, its guardrails, its tool set, and the reach of the project service agent, and no single console screen shows that union. Because tools execute with the platform identity, an agent that looks harmless in isolation can inherit the full backend reach of every other tool in its project, which only a review that considers the project as a whole will catch.
Notes: The review covers at minimum: the tool list and what each tool can reach, guardrail configuration, whether any data store grounds the agent on content narrower in audience than the agent itself, the deployment channel and whether it permits anonymous access, and whether the agent handles determination-bearing content that requires a human decision maker. Record the approval as certification evidence.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (Risk Analysis), 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-4 (Impact Analyses), SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: Agent evaluations **MUST** be executed and reviewed against a documented test set before an agent application is promoted to production, and after any change to its instructions, tools, or guardrails.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio provides an evaluation capability with import and export of evaluation data, which makes a regression test set a supported artifact rather than an aspiration. Agent behaviour is emergent rather than specified, so a change to instructions intended to improve one interaction can silently alter refusal behaviour, tool selection, or disclosure in another, and only a held test set will detect it.
Notes: The test set must include adversarial cases, not only happy paths: prompt injection attempts, requests for information the agent should refuse, and attempts to induce a tool call the caller is not entitled to. Evaluation operations may appear on the v1beta API surface, which this guide restricts to non-production projects, so run evaluations there and promote only the reviewed configuration.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-4 (Impact Analyses), SI-10 (Information Input Validation); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM01 (Prompt Injection)

Requirement: Agent applications **MUST NOT** be the sole authority for a coverage, eligibility, clinical, or other adverse determination communicated to a member.
Rationale: A generative agent produces a fluent answer whether or not the underlying retrieval succeeded, and this suite provides no mechanism that distinguishes a grounded answer from a plausible one at the point of delivery. An adverse determination carries regulatory notice, appeal, and accuracy obligations that attach to the organization regardless of which system produced the text.
Notes: Constrain member-facing agents to informational responses and route determination-bearing interactions to a human with the agent acting as an assistant. Where an agent surfaces a determination made elsewhere, it must present the determination reached by the system of record rather than restating it in generated language.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI), 164.520 (Notice of Privacy Practices); NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM09 (Misinformation); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI09 (Human-Agent Trust Exploitation)

Requirement: Members interacting with a Gemini Enterprise for CX agent **MUST** be informed that they are interacting with an automated agent and offered a path to reach a human.
Rationale: Disclosure of automated interaction is a growing statutory obligation across US states and a settled expectation in healthcare member communication. The suite's own design assumes escalation - the Prompt guard offers agent handoff as a triggered outcome and Agent Assist exists to support the human who receives the escalation - so the path is available and needs only to be configured and disclosed.
Notes: Configure the fallback behaviour and the Prompt guard outcome so that escalation is a real destination rather than a dead end, and confirm the human receiving the handoff has the conversation context. Verify the disclosure appears on every approved deployment channel, including voice, where it must be spoken rather than displayed.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.520 (Notice of Privacy Practices); NIST 800-53: PT-5 (Privacy Notice), PT-4 (Consent), AC-3 (Access Enforcement)

Requirement: Agent applications generated by the Start with AI capability **MUST** be reviewed in full, including their generated instructions and tools, before deployment.
Rationale: Start with AI generates a starter agent and its tools from supplied documentation, which means both the agent's instructions and its tool registrations are model output rather than a human design. The generated tool set in particular determines what the agent can reach, and it is produced by inference over documentation rather than by an authorization decision.
Notes: Treat the generated artifact as a draft. The standard pre-deployment agent security review applies unchanged, with additional attention to tools the generator created that no one requested. This capability reached GA with the February 4, 2026 launch, so the prohibition here is about review discipline rather than launch stage.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation), AC-6 (Least Privilege), CM-4 (Impact Analyses)

Requirement: Where one agent application is registered as a tool of another, the delegation chain **MUST** be documented and reviewed as a single authorization surface.
Rationale: Agents as tools became generally available on April 17, 2026 and allows an agent to invoke another agent. Because tools execute with the project service agent's permissions, a delegation chain does not narrow authority at each hop - the invoked agent reaches everything the service agent reaches, regardless of what the caller was entitled to. A chain therefore aggregates rather than attenuates reach, and reviewing either agent alone will not reveal it.
Notes: Record the full graph of which agents invoke which, and review the union of tools reachable through the graph rather than the tool list of any single agent. A cycle or a chain crossing a trust boundary is a finding. This is the strongest single argument for separating projects by trust domain.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM06 (Excessive Agency); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI07 (Insecure Inter-Agent Communication); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0053 (AI Agent Tool Invocation)

Requirement: Agent versioning and changelog history **SHOULD** be retained for the life of the agent application.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio provides granular changelogs and rollback as a product capability. That history is the only record of what an agent was instructed to do at a given moment, which is what an incident investigation, a member complaint, or a regulatory inquiry will ask about. Conversation transcripts alone do not answer why the agent said what it said.
Notes: Where an investigation may need to reconstruct behaviour beyond the retained changelog window, export the agent configuration on a schedule and retain the exports under the organization's records retention policy. Rollback is also the fastest containment action for a bad agent change, so exercise it at least once before relying on it in an incident. Do not prune changelog history as part of routine housekeeping - it is the only record of what an agent was instructed to do at a given moment.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls); NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), CP-9 (System Backup)

Requirement: Only models on the organization's approved model allowlist **MUST** be selected to power a Gemini Enterprise for CX agent application.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio exposes a model picker offering several Gemini variants, and the choice determines the reasoning quality, the safety behaviour, and the latency of every member conversation the agent handles. Google states that CX Agent Studio models are performance-tuned for customer experience and may differ from the standard Vertex AI offering of the same name, so a model's behaviour here cannot be inferred from testing it elsewhere. Without an allowlist the model is whatever the builder picked from a dropdown, and it changes silently whenever Google revises the list.
Notes: Maintain the allowlist as an explicit artifact naming each approved model and the date its launch stage was checked, and reconcile it against the picker at the monthly release-note review. Voice-optimized and text-optimized models are separate entries and need separate approval, because a voice deployment reaches a different model than the text deployment of the same agent.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), SA-4 (Acquisition Process); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM03 (Supply Chain); NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1): GOVERN, MAP

Requirement: A model designated Preview in the CX Agent Studio model picker **MUST NOT** be selected for an agent application carrying production traffic.
Rationale: Google marks at least one model in the picker as Preview while presenting it alongside generally available models in the same dropdown, with no separation in the interface. A Preview model is governed by the Pre-GA Offerings Terms: no production SLA, changeable or withdrawable without notice, and not necessarily inside the compliance certifications the deployment relies on. A builder selecting it is making a contractual and compliance decision through a dropdown that gives no indication one was made.
Notes: At the time of authoring the Preview entry was gemini-3-flash, with gemini-3.7-flash, gemini-3.5-flash, gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-3.1-flash-live shown as generally available. Verify the current designations in the picker rather than relying on that list, because the composition changes without a release note. Enforce by reviewing the selected model during the pre-deployment agent security review.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles)

Requirement: A model override applied to an individual sub-agent **MUST** be documented and approved as a change to the agent application.
Rationale: Google states that a global model can be set for the agent application and overridden for specific sub-agents. An override is invisible from the application-level configuration, so an agent reviewed and approved on one model can contain a sub-agent running on another, including one that is Preview or not on the allowlist. Because sub-agents frequently handle the narrower and more sensitive parts of a conversation, the override lands precisely where it matters most.
Notes: Enumerate sub-agent model assignments explicitly during review rather than reading the application-level setting alone, and record the effective model per sub-agent in the configuration baseline so the quarterly drift check can detect a change.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), CM-4 (Impact Analyses); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM03 (Supply Chain)

Requirement: The launch stage of a selected model **MUST** be verified in the CX Agent Studio interface rather than inferred from that model's status in other Google Cloud products.
Rationale: Google states that all models in CX Agent Studio are considered generally available unless explicitly marked Preview in the interface, and that this launch stage is specific to CX Agent Studio and operates independently of a model's status in other Google Cloud products. A model that is generally available in Vertex AI may therefore be Preview here, and the reverse also holds. An engineer checking the model's status on its Vertex AI documentation page will reach a conclusion that does not govern this product.
Notes: This is the reason the allowlist records where and when each launch stage was checked. Treat the CX Agent Studio picker as the only authoritative source for a model's stage within this product, and re-verify at each monthly release-note review rather than at model selection alone.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

Requirement: Each Gemini Enterprise for CX project **MUST** contain only agent applications that share a single trust domain.
Rationale: Google states that OpenAPI tool actions execute with the permissions granted to the CX Agent Studio service account rather than the end user's, and that service agent is a single identity per project. The effective reach of any agent in a project is therefore the union of every backend any tool in that project authenticates to, and no in-product setting narrows it. Combined with the Google-hosted token broker's anonymous access path, the worst plausible configuration is an unauthenticated caller whose reach is that entire union. The project boundary is the only real boundary this product offers.
Notes: This decision is made before the first agent application exists and is expensive to reverse, because moving an agent means recreating it, its tools, its deployment channels, and its data stores in a new project with a new perimeter. Google names dedicated projects as its own first recommended mitigation. Where a shared project is proposed for cost or operational reasons, the residual risk to accept is explicitly that every agent in it can reach every backend any of its tools reach. Agents serving different audiences or reaching different sensitivity tiers belong in separate projects, because the project is the scope of the service agent whose permissions every tool executes with.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management); NIST 800-53: AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API5 (Broken Function Level Authorization); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI03 (Identity and Privilege Abuse); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0053 (AI Agent Tool Invocation)

Requirement: An inventory of every registered tool, its type, its target system, its authentication method, and its approving owner **MUST** be maintained and reviewed at least quarterly.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio offers sixteen tool types spanning arbitrary HTTP APIs, MCP servers, SaaS connectors, data stores, and code execution, and any holder of the toolsEditor role can register one without a deployment. Because a registered tool immediately extends what agents in the project can reach, an unmaintained inventory means the project's effective reach is unknown to the people accountable for it.
Notes: The inventory is the input to the project-boundary judgement, so it must record what each tool can reach rather than only what it is called. Tool registration and modification appear in Data Access audit logs under `ces.googleapis.com` and should be alerted on so the inventory can be reconciled against actual changes.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-8 (System Component Inventory), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), AC-6 (Least Privilege), SA-9 (External System Services)

Requirement: Credentials used by OpenAPI and MCP tools **MUST** be stored in Secret Manager and referenced rather than embedded in tool configuration, agent instructions, or custom header values.
Rationale: Google documents Secret Manager as the supported credential store for OpenAPI tools, with Secret Manager Secret Accessor granted to the CX Agent Studio service agent, and states that MCP tools carry the same authentication options. A credential held anywhere else in the product is readable by every holder of the viewer role, travels in configuration exports, and has no rotation or access-audit path of its own.
Notes: MCP custom header values must be supplied by variables, which makes it tempting to place a static token in a variable - do not. Reference a Secret Manager secret instead. Note the perimeter interaction: Google documents that OpenAPI tools cannot reference authentication keys using secrets outside the VPC Service Controls perimeter, so the secret and the perimeter must be planned together.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(i) (Unique User Identification); NIST 800-53: IA-5 (Authenticator Management), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Requirement: A tool **MUST NOT** be granted access to a backend system whose data population is broader than the audience authorized to converse with the agents in that project.
Rationale: Because the tool executes as the project service agent and not as the caller, backend authorization is applied to the platform identity rather than to the member. A tool wired to an API that can return any member's record will return any member's record when the model is persuaded to ask for one, and no guardrail reliably prevents that because the request is a legitimate tool call.
Notes: Where per-member scoping is required, it must be enforced in the backend API by binding the request to a verified member identifier that the agent cannot choose freely - a session-bound identifier established at authentication, not a value the model extracts from the conversation. If the backend cannot do that, the tool is not eligible for a member-facing agent. This is the concrete form of the confused-deputy exposure that makes the project boundary the real security boundary in this product.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI02 (Tool Misuse and Exploitation); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0053 (AI Agent Tool Invocation)

Requirement: Data store tools **MUST NOT** be grounded on content whose authorized audience is narrower than the audience able to converse with the agent.
Rationale: The data store tool documentation describes grounding on website and uploaded content and is silent on access-control-aware retrieval, per-user result filtering, and the identity under which retrieval executes. Absent a documented ACL-aware retrieval path, the safe reading is that any content ingested into a data store is reachable by any caller who can reach the agent, and the grounding score setting does not change who can see what.
Notes: Curate corpora to the agent's audience rather than relying on retrieval to filter. For a member-facing agent this means public and member-general content only - no internal policy documents, no case notes, no provider-specific material. Note the regional pinning constraint: once a data store from one region is added to a tool, only data stores from that same region can be added to it.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AC-21 (Information Sharing), AC-6 (Least Privilege); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure)

Requirement: Content ingested into a data store used by a member-facing agent **MUST** be reviewed and approved before ingestion, and limited to sources under the organization's control.
Rationale: Retrieved content enters the model's context and is acted upon as instruction-bearing input. Where a corpus includes externally authored material - a crawled website, a vendor document, a partner feed - an attacker who can edit that source has a durable indirect prompt injection path into every conversation the corpus grounds, without ever interacting with the agent.
Notes: Website data stores are the highest-risk case because the crawl re-ingests whatever the page currently says. Restrict website data stores to domains the organization controls, and re-review third-party content on a defined cadence rather than treating ingestion as one-time. This requirement addresses the injection vector; the untrusted-input requirement addresses what the agent does with the result.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection), SR-3 (Supply Chain Controls and Processes), CM-8 (System Component Inventory); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM01 (Prompt Injection); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI06 (Memory and Context Poisoning); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0051.001 (LLM Prompt Injection - Indirect)

Requirement: Tool responses, retrieved data store content, and knowledge base excerpts **MUST** be treated as untrusted input that cannot authorize a subsequent action the caller could not authorize directly.
Rationale: Every source that enters the model context is a channel through which an instruction can arrive, and the model does not distinguish retrieved text from a member's utterance. An agent that will call a second tool because the first tool's response told it to has delegated its authorization decision to whoever controls that backend's response body, which in a multi-hop or third-party integration is not the organization.
Notes: Enforce architecturally rather than through prompt engineering: constrain which tools an agent may call and in what sequence, and require any state-changing action to be gated on a condition established outside the model's context. The Prompt guard reduces the frequency of successful injection; it does not bound the consequence.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SI-15 (Information Output Filtering); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM01 (Prompt Injection), LLM06 (Excessive Agency); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI01 (Agent Goal Hijack), ASI06 (Memory and Context Poisoning); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0051.001 (LLM Prompt Injection - Indirect), AML.T0053 (AI Agent Tool Invocation)

Requirement: Third-party and externally hosted MCP servers **MUST** pass a supply chain security review before being registered as a tool.
Rationale: Google documents that MCP tools may target prebuilt servers, servers built with third-party frameworks, or servers deployed by the customer, and that they carry the same authentication options as OpenAPI tools - meaning they too execute with the project service agent's permissions. An MCP server also declares its own tool definitions, so a compromised or malicious server controls both the description the model reasons over and the response it acts on.
Notes: The review covers who operates the server, how its tool definitions are versioned and change-controlled, what it logs, and whether its declared tools can change after registration. Only StreamableHttpTransport servers are supported; SSE transport servers are not, so a server offering only SSE cannot be used regardless of review outcome. An unreviewed public MCP server is never eligible for registration regardless of how convenient its tool set appears.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), SR-3 (Supply Chain Controls and Processes), SR-11 (Component Authenticity), CM-7 (Least Functionality); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM03 (Supply Chain); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI04 (Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0110 (AI Agent Tool Poisoning)

Requirement: MCP servers used by production agent applications **SHOULD** be hosted within the organization's Google Cloud boundary, with invocation restricted to the CX Agent Studio service agent.
Rationale: Google's documented pattern hosts the MCP server on Cloud Run and grants the Cloud Run Invoker role to `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-ces.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. That arrangement keeps the tool definitions under the organization's change control, keeps conversation-derived parameters inside the boundary, and makes the server's own logs available for investigation - none of which holds for a server operated by a third party.
Notes: Restricting the Invoker role to the service agent alone also prevents the MCP server becoming an unauthenticated internal API. Combined with a VPC Service Controls perimeter, a Cloud Run MCP server inside that perimeter is reachable only through the agent path. Test the server independently with curl or Postman before registration, as Google recommends.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SA-9 (External System Services), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM03 (Supply Chain)

Requirement: Integration Connector tools for Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Confluence, and SharePoint **MUST** authenticate with a dedicated connection identity scoped to the minimum records the agent requires.
Rationale: These connectors reach systems that hold case notes, ticket bodies, and document libraries whose contents routinely include member-identifying detail written by staff for staff. Because retrieval through the tool is not user-scoped, the connection identity's entitlements become the agent's entitlements, and a connection created with an administrator's profile exposes the entire system through a conversational interface.
Notes: Create a purpose-built integration account in each SaaS platform rather than reusing an existing service or personal account, and scope it at the source system with object, field, and record filters. Re-verify scope after any change to the source system's permission model, which is outside Google Cloud's change control and will not surface in a CX Agent Studio review.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts); NIST 800-53: AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SA-9 (External System Services), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization)

Requirement: Python code tools **MUST** be reviewed as application source code before registration and before any subsequent modification.
Rationale: A Python code tool is arbitrary executable logic invoked as part of a conversation, which places it in the same risk class as application code while offering none of the surrounding pipeline controls - no branch protection, no peer review gate, no dependency scanning, no build provenance. The vendor documentation for this tool type could not be retrieved during authoring, so its execution environment, isolation properties, and egress behaviour are not established.
Notes: Because the execution model is undocumented, do not assume sandboxing, network isolation, or credential isolation from the service agent. Treat the code as running with the project service agent's reach until Google documents otherwise. Review for outbound network calls, credential handling, and unbounded input handling. Verify the execution model directly with Google before this tool type is used with member data. A production modification without the same review is a change to executable logic in the conversation path and is not permitted.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation), SA-15 (Development Process, Standards, and Tools), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity), CM-7 (Least Functionality); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM05 (Improper Output Handling); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI05 (Unexpected Code Execution)

Requirement: Client function tools **MUST NOT** be passed data that the end user is not already authorized to see.
Rationale: A client function tool executes in the calling client rather than on the platform, so every parameter passed to it crosses to the end user's device. On the web widget that device is an untrusted browser, and on a public deployment it may belong to an unauthenticated party. Data placed in a client function call is disclosed at the moment of the call regardless of what the function does with it.
Notes: The vendor page for this tool type could not be retrieved during authoring, so the parameter-passing detail rests on the tool's placement in the tool taxonomy and its name. Verify the data flow directly before using client function tools on any member-facing channel, and in the interim restrict them to values the member supplied in the same conversation.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-8 (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure)

Requirement: The Google Search tool **SHOULD NOT** be enabled on member-facing agent applications.
Rationale: Grounding a member conversation on open web results introduces content the organization neither authored nor controls into a channel members treat as authoritative, and it sends conversation-derived query terms outside the assessed boundary. For health and benefits questions the accuracy and provenance obligations sit with the organization no matter where the text originated.
Notes: Where broad knowledge is genuinely needed, a curated and reviewed data store provides grounding the organization can review and version. If the Search tool is required for a specific internal-facing use case, document the query terms that can reach it and confirm they carry no member identifiers.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SC-7 (Boundary Protection); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM09 (Misinformation)

Requirement: OpenAPI tools **MUST NOT** target endpoints reachable only over the public internet where a private path through Service Directory is available.
Rationale: Google documents Service Directory private network access as the supported way for CX Agent Studio to reach OpenAPI tool targets inside a VPC network, stating that this keeps traffic within the Google Cloud network and enforces IAM and VPC Service Controls. A tool that egresses to a public endpoint instead forfeits all three properties for every conversation parameter it carries.
Notes: Configure Service Directory private network access and grant `servicedirectory.viewer` and `servicedirectory.pscAuthorizedService` to `service-agent-project-number@gcp-sa-ces.iam.gserviceaccount.com`; where Service Directory lives in a different project, grant `servicedirectory.viewer` in both. Note that within a perimeter this stops being a preference - Google documents that tools and callbacks cannot send requests to arbitrary HTTP endpoints once VPC Service Controls is enabled without Service Directory configuration.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-8 (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity)

Requirement: The set of tools registered in a project **MUST** be restricted to those the approved agent use cases require, with unused registrations removed.
Rationale: Because tool authority aggregates at the project service agent rather than attenuating per agent, every registered tool that no agent needs is pure added blast radius. Tools also accumulate during development and vendor-led enablement sessions and are rarely removed, so the gap between what is registered and what is used widens silently over time.
Notes: Reconcile the tool inventory against actual tool invocation observed in conversation history and audit logs on the quarterly cycle. A tool registered but never invoked in a full quarter is a candidate for removal, and its continued presence should require a stated reason.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-8 (System Component Inventory), AC-6 (Least Privilege), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM06 (Excessive Agency); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI02 (Tool Misuse and Exploitation)

Requirement: Tool invocations **MUST** carry a correlation identifier, comprising at minimum the agent application identifier and the conversation or session identifier, that the receiving backend system records in its own logs.
Rationale: Every tool call reaches the backend as the single CX Agent Studio service agent, so the backend's own audit log records one identity for every agent, every conversation, and every member in the project. Without a correlation identifier the backend cannot attribute an action to the conversation that caused it, which means an investigation starting from a backend record - a changed claim, an unexpected lookup, an anomalous query volume - has no path back into the conversation history. The Google Cloud side of the boundary is well instrumented; the identifier is what carries that attribution across it.
Notes: Pass the identifier as a request header or a defined request field on OpenAPI, MCP, and Integration Connector tools, and require the receiving system to log it as a condition of being connected. The identifier is metadata rather than content and must not carry member identifiers or conversation text. This is the control that makes the confused-deputy residual risk investigable after the fact rather than merely accepted.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review); NIST 800-53: AU-3 (Content of Audit Records), AU-2 (Event Logging), IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication), AC-3 (Access Enforcement); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI03 (Identity and Privilege Abuse); MITRE ATLAS: AML.T0053 (AI Agent Tool Invocation)

Requirement: An inventory of every deployment channel, its authentication mode, and its approving owner **MUST** be maintained for each agent application.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio publishes an agent to seven distinct surfaces - web widget, AudioCodes, Five9, Google Cloud CCaaS, Google Telephony Platform, Twilio, and direct API access - and each carries a different authentication model and a different population of callers. The security posture of an agent is meaningless without knowing which of these it is exposed on, and a channel added later does not change anything visible in the agent's own configuration.
Notes: The inventory records, per channel, whether callers are authenticated, what identity the channel's token carries, and which third party operates the transport. It should reconcile exactly against the holders of the query-access client role, because every channel needs one and nothing else legitimately does.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-8 (System Component Inventory), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures)

Requirement: Public access through the Google-hosted token broker **MUST NOT** be enabled for any agent application whose tools can reach member data.
Rationale: Google documents the Google-hosted token broker as the mechanism that allows public access to a chat widget, which means an unauthenticated caller obtains a valid token and converses with the agent. Because tools execute with the project service agent's permissions rather than the caller's, the effective reach of that anonymous conversation is every backend any tool in the project authenticates to. Anonymous access and service-agent tool execution are individually defensible and jointly a direct path from the open internet to member records.
Notes: Where a genuinely public agent is required - a benefits FAQ or a store locator - place it in its own project with its own service agent and no tool that reaches member data, so that anonymous reach is bounded by the project rather than by the agent's instructions. This is the single highest-value application of the dedicated-project rule in this guide.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), IA-8 (Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users)), AC-6 (Least Privilege), SC-7 (Boundary Protection); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API2 (Broken Authentication), API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization)

Requirement: Where public access is approved for a bounded public-information agent, origin checks and reCAPTCHA **MUST** both be enabled on the widget configuration.
Rationale: Google presents these as optional additions - the documentation reads enable public access, and optionally enable origin and reCAPTCHA checks, recommended to prevent spoofing and abuse. Left at their defaults they are off, which leaves a publicly reachable generative endpoint with no origin binding and no automation control: it can be embedded on any site, driven by a script, and consumed as a free inference endpoint at the organization's expense.
Notes: Origin checks bind the widget to the organization's own pages, which is what makes an embedded agent attributable. reCAPTCHA constrains automated abuse. Neither is a substitute for the reach limitation that comes from a dedicated project with no sensitive tools, and both must be verified after any widget configuration change because they sit in the same form as the public-access toggle.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-5 (Denial-of-service Protection), SC-23 (Session Authenticity), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM10 (Unbounded Consumption); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API4 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption), API2 (Broken Authentication)

Requirement: Agent applications serving authenticated members **MUST** use the OAuth2 client end-user authentication path rather than a service-account token broker.
Rationale: The widget supports an OAuth2 client that authenticates the end user and returns a token operating on that user's behalf, and Google notes that the identity associated with the token - end user or service account - must hold the IAM permissions to interact with the agent. A service-account broker makes every member session indistinguishable at the platform layer, so the conversation record cannot be attributed and no per-member condition can be applied at the boundary.
Notes: End-user authentication authenticates the caller to the platform; it does not make tool execution user-scoped, which remains the service agent's. Per-member data scoping must still be enforced in the backend API against a session-bound identifier. Configure authorized JavaScript origins and redirect URIs to the organization's domains only.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)), IA-8 (Identification and Authentication (Non-organizational Users)), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API2 (Broken Authentication)

Requirement: A self-hosted token broker **SHOULD** be used in preference to the Google-hosted broker for any agent application handling member interactions.
Rationale: A self-hosted broker runs in the organization's own project on Cloud Run, which puts token issuance under the organization's logging, rate limiting, IP controls, and change management. The Google-hosted broker exists to enable public access and offers no place to apply an organization-specific condition before a token is minted.
Notes: Google publishes sample code for the self-hosted broker. Its service account should hold only the query-access client role and nothing else, and it needs no downloaded key because Cloud Run attaches the identity. Broker request logs are useful evidence of who initiated a conversation and when.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(d) (Person or Entity Authentication); NIST 800-53: IA-5 (Authenticator Management), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AU-2 (Event Logging)

Requirement: The web widget **MUST** be embedded only on web origins the organization controls.
Rationale: The widget is deployed as an HTML snippet, which is copyable and will function wherever it is pasted unless origin checks constrain it. An agent embedded on a third-party or attacker-controlled page presents the organization's brand and voice in a context the organization cannot vouch for, and any data the member provides transits a page the organization does not control.
Notes: Enforce with the widget's origin check rather than by policy alone, and maintain the approved origin list as configuration under change control. Review it whenever a partner or vendor site is added, since an origin approved for a marketing campaign rarely gets removed afterwards.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-23 (Session Authenticity), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SC-7 (Boundary Protection)

Requirement: Non-production agent development and testing **MUST** be performed in a separate Google Cloud project from production, using deployment environments that carry no production traffic.
Rationale: Testing an agent means driving it with realistic input against realistic tools, and in a shared project that means the test agent inherits the production service agent's reach into production backends. Deployment environments separate versions within a project but do not separate the identity that tools execute as, so the environment feature alone does not create the boundary.
Notes: Non-production projects should carry synthetic conversation data rather than copies of member conversations. This is also where the pre-release v1beta and v1alpha1 API surfaces belong, since evaluation capabilities that are only offered there can be exercised without placing production traffic on an unsupported API version.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(4)(ii)(B) (Access Authorization), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation)

Requirement: Traffic splitting **MUST NOT** direct production conversations to an agent version that has not completed security review and evaluation.
Rationale: Traffic splitting became generally available on July 1, 2026 and directs a configured share of live traffic to an alternate version. It is an experimentation control rather than a release control, so it will happily place real member conversations on an unreviewed configuration, and the change is made by a deployment editor without touching the agent's own changelog.
Notes: Require that every version participating in a split has passed review and evaluation, so the split decides how much traffic a version receives rather than whether an unreviewed version receives any. Split configuration changes appear in Admin Activity audit logs and are worth alerting on.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-4 (Impact Analyses), SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation), AU-2 (Event Logging)

Requirement: Third-party contact centre platforms connected as deployment channels - AudioCodes, Five9, Twilio, and any comparable provider - **MUST** have completed a third-party security assessment and, where they process ePHI, be covered by an executed business associate agreement.
Rationale: These platforms carry the full audio and text of member conversations between the member and the agent, which places them squarely in the ePHI path as business associates. Google's BAA covers Google Cloud services; it does not extend to a telephony or CCaaS provider the organization contracts with separately, so the contractual chain has a gap unless the organization closes it directly.
Notes: Assess the recording, retention, and subprocessor posture of each provider, not only its transport encryption, because these platforms frequently retain their own copy of call audio on their own schedule. Confirm which party holds the recording of record and where it is stored, since that copy is usually outside every control in this guide.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.314(a) (Business Associate Contracts or Other Arrangements), 164.502(e) (Disclosures to Business Associates); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), SR-3 (Supply Chain Controls and Processes), CA-3 (Information Exchange), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: Direct API access to deployed agent applications **MUST** be routed through the organization's API gateway rather than exposed to callers as a direct Google endpoint.
Rationale: The API channel is a conversational inference endpoint reachable by anything holding a query-access token, and the product provides no rate limiting, quota policy, request logging, or payload inspection of its own at that boundary. Fronting it with the gateway is what makes throttling, authorization policy, and request-level logging available for a surface that otherwise has none.
Notes: The gateway is also the enforcement point for any per-caller authorization the backend cannot express, and its access logs are the only record of API-channel conversations that exists independently of Google's own logging. Apply the same rate limits to internal callers as to external ones - a runaway internal integration produces the same cost and the same load.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-5 (Denial-of-service Protection), AU-2 (Event Logging); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM10 (Unbounded Consumption); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API4 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption), API2 (Broken Authentication)

Requirement: Voice channels **MUST** present a recording and automated-interaction disclosure to the member before conversation content is captured.
Rationale: Every voice deployment path in this suite results in call audio being captured, transcribed, retained in Cloud Storage, and analysed in CX Insights. Recording consent is governed by state law with two-party consent jurisdictions imposing the stricter standard, and the disclosure must precede capture rather than accompany it, because the obligation attaches at the moment audio is retained.
Notes: The disclosure must cover both recording and the automated nature of the agent, and it must be spoken on voice channels rather than assumed from a web page. Where a third-party platform plays the disclosure, confirm that it does so before audio reaches Google Cloud, not after.
