Mappings: HIPAA: 164.520 (Notice of Privacy Practices), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: PT-4 (Consent), PT-5 (Privacy Notice), PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information)

Requirement: Quota caps and cost alerting **MUST** be configured for every agent application exposed on a public or high-volume deployment channel.
Rationale: An agent application is a metered generative inference endpoint, and the web widget can be configured for anonymous public access. An attacker, a misconfigured integration, or a runaway retry loop consumes model capacity and incurs cost at a rate bounded only by the platform's own quotas, and the failure is financial and availability-affecting before it is ever a confidentiality problem. The organization's API gateway constrains the API channel but sits nowhere in the path of the web widget or the telephony connections.
Notes: Set caps per deployment rather than per project so one channel cannot exhaust the capacity of another, and alert on rate of spend rather than absolute spend so a change in pattern surfaces within hours rather than at the end of the billing period. Origin checks and reCAPTCHA reduce the frequency of automated abuse on the widget but place no ceiling on it.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-5 (Denial-of-service Protection), SI-4 (System Monitoring), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CP-2 (Contingency Plan); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM10 (Unbounded Consumption); OWASP API Top 10 2023: API4 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption)

Requirement: Customer-managed encryption keys **MUST** be initialized for Agent Assist before it processes any production conversation.
Rationale: Agent Assist maintains its own CMEK initialization separate from CX Agent Studio and CX Insights, so a project can be fully CMEK-covered on two components and unprotected on the third. Agent Assist holds live conversation transcripts, generated summaries, and knowledge excerpts, which is the same class of content the other two components protect.
Notes: Immutable at first use: Google states "You cannot change encryption key settings for a location once it has been specified" and that a project already holding Agent Assist data in a location cannot have a key added for that location. Initialize through the InitializeEncryptionSpec API and grant Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter to service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-ccai-cmek.iam.gserviceaccount.com. Coverage is not total: Google states "CMEK is not available for features that are disabled in Agent Assist locations and smart reply", so Smart Reply data is outside the customer-key boundary even in a fully CMEK-configured project. Record that exclusion in the data flow record and weigh it when deciding whether Smart Reply is enabled at all.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.312(e)(2)(ii) (Encryption); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-28(1) (Cryptographic Protection), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management)

Requirement: Sensitive Data Protection redaction **MUST** be configured for Agent Assist conversation data using an inspect template and a deidentify template.
Rationale: Agent Assist operates on live conversation content in which members state identifiers, conditions, and payment details conversationally rather than in structured fields. Redaction configured through DLP templates is the mechanism that scrubs those values before persistence, and without it the raw utterance is what is stored, analysed, and later exported.
Notes: Redaction fails open and is bound per conversation profile, not per project: Google states "You must specify the security settings to apply for each conversation profile" and that "If you don't specify any security settings in a conversation profile, Agent Assist doesn't apply any redaction for that conversation profile." Security settings are created once per project and location but take effect only where attached, so verification means enumerating every conversation profile and confirming an attachment on each - a project can satisfy the template half of this requirement completely and still store unredacted transcripts. The inspect template defines what constitutes sensitive data and the deidentify template defines how it is masked or removed; both must be tuned against real transcripts because contact centre language differs substantially from the document text DLP detectors are usually calibrated on. Note that a redaction template located outside a VPC Service Controls perimeter causes redaction failures rather than degrading gracefully.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.514(a) (De-identification of PHI), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SI-18 (Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-7 (Boundary Protection)

Requirement: Agent Assist conversation data retention **MUST** be configured to the shortest period that meets a documented business need.
Rationale: Google documents conversation data as regionalized, logically isolated, and retained for a configurable period defaulting to one year with a two-year maximum. A default retention of one year across an entire contact centre's traffic accumulates a very large corpus of member conversation whose only justification is that nobody chose a number.
Notes: Set retention deliberately against a stated business and records-retention rationale rather than against the maximum the product allows. Where quality review and dispute resolution need a longer window than routine operations, scope the longer period to the conversations that need it rather than raising the floor for all of them. Google documents that in Agent Assist "The default and maximum retention window is 30 days", set through retention_window_days in the project-and-location security settings. Thirty days is a ceiling rather than a starting point, so the practical work of this requirement is confirming that quality review, dispute resolution, and any downstream export can operate inside it - a business need longer than 30 days cannot be met by changing this setting and must be met by exporting to a store the organization controls.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), MP-6 (Media Sanitization)

Requirement: Generated conversation summaries **MUST** be reviewed by the human representative before they are committed to a system of record.
Rationale: A summarization model produces a fluent account of the conversation whether or not it captured the material facts, and it may omit a commitment made to the member or attribute a statement to the wrong party. Once a summary is written into a case, a claim note, or a service record, it becomes the organization's account of the interaction and is relied on by every downstream reader.
Notes: The reviewing representative needs the transcript alongside the summary and a genuine ability to edit it, not merely to accept it. Where summaries are written automatically with no human step, they must be labelled as machine-generated in the record so a later reader can weigh them accordingly.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(c)(1) (Integrity), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SI-15 (Information Output Filtering), AU-3 (Content of Audit Records); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM09 (Misinformation)

Requirement: Smart Reply and generated response suggestions **MUST NOT** be transmitted to a member without an affirmative action by the human representative.
Rationale: Smart Reply supplies candidate responses drawn from the model's reading of the conversation, and a suggestion that is accurate in most cases will be wrong in some. Auto-sending removes the only check in the path, and the resulting message reaches the member carrying the organization's authority with no one having read it.
Notes: Affirmative means a deliberate send action, not a timeout that sends by default and not a single click that both accepts and transmits without displaying the text. Confirm the behaviour in the deployed UI module rather than in the product description, because the integration layer determines what the representative actually sees.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI), 164.312(c)(1) (Integrity); NIST 800-53: SI-15 (Information Output Filtering), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SI-10 (Information Input Validation); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM06 (Excessive Agency); OWASP Agentic Top 10 2025: ASI09 (Human-Agent Trust Exploitation)

Requirement: Knowledge bases used by Knowledge Assist and Generative Knowledge Assist **MUST** be scoped to content the entire representative population is authorized to see.
Rationale: Knowledge Assist surfaces excerpts from the configured knowledge base directly in the representative's workspace during a live call, and there is no per-representative filtering of what the retrieval can return. Any document in the corpus is therefore visible to every representative the moment a conversation makes it relevant, regardless of the access controls that governed it in its original location.
Notes: Review the corpus against the representative population rather than against the author's intent. Material scoped to clinical staff, legal, or a specific business unit does not belong in a general contact centre knowledge base, and its presence there is a disclosure that no access review of the source system will detect. Content restricted to a narrower audience must be excluded from the corpus entirely, since retrieval applies no per-representative filter.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-21 (Information Sharing), AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)

Requirement: Live Translation output **MUST NOT** be relied upon as the authoritative record of a member interaction.
Rationale: Machine translation of a live conversation about benefits, coverage, or clinical detail can invert meaning in ways neither party detects, because neither participant reads both languages. If only the translated text is retained, the organization holds no record of what the member actually said and cannot reconstruct the interaction in a dispute or a grievance.
Notes: Retain source-language transcript alongside the translation and mark translated turns. Where the interaction determines a benefit or a clinical pathway, a qualified human interpreter remains the appropriate mechanism, and language access obligations are not satisfied by a machine translation feature. Retain the source-language content alongside the translation and mark translated turns, so the interaction can be reconstructed in a dispute.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(c)(1) (Integrity), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: SI-10 (Information Input Validation), AU-3 (Content of Audit Records), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention); OWASP LLM Top 10 2025: LLM09 (Misinformation)

Requirement: Agent Assist deployments **MUST** be pinned to a region consistent with the organization's data residency position, with per-feature residency coverage verified before enablement.
Rationale: Agent Assist maintains its own regionalization documentation separate from CX Agent Studio's two multi-regions and CX Insights' region list, which means the three components can be pinned inconsistently and produce a data path that crosses a boundary the organization believes it has closed. Generative features in particular have historically had narrower regional availability than the products that host them.
Notes: Two documented limitations shape this choice. Google notes that Vertex AI does not support the us multi-region, so "using Agent Assist's Generative AI features in 'us' multi-region will rely on the respective existing US single region endpoints" - pinning Agent Assist to us does not keep generative processing in the multi-region, and does not produce the same processing locality as the CX Agent Studio us multi-region pin elsewhere in this guide. Separately, the AI/ML data location commitment "is only supported in locations in the US and EU", and "For non-AI/ML data (in use or transit) or data outside US and EU multi-regions, the DRZ commitment doesn't apply" - residency is a data-at-rest guarantee, not an in-use or in-transit one. Record the region, the per-feature availability table, and both limitations as certification evidence before enablement.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SA-9(5) (Processing, Storage, and Service Location), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SA-9 (External System Services)

Requirement: Where AI Coach, quality scoring, or comparable Agent Assist capabilities evaluate the performance of a human representative, that evaluation **MUST** be governed by the organization's employee monitoring and workforce policy before enablement.
Rationale: AI Coach delivers real-time guidance and coaching, and the analytics layer generates assessments of representative performance from the same conversation corpus. That combination is continuous algorithmic evaluation of identified employees, which carries notice obligations, consultation expectations in some jurisdictions, and a fairness and contestability obligation that sits outside the security review.
Notes: Confirm before enablement who can see an individual's scores, how long they are retained, whether they feed employment decisions, and what the appeal path is. The technical controls in this guide protect the conversation data; they say nothing about the appropriateness of the evaluation built on top of it, which is a separate approval.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information), PT-5 (Privacy Notice), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: The Agent Assist Build your own assist capability **MUST NOT** be enabled while it is designated Preview.
Rationale: Google's Agent Assist regional feature table lists Build your own assist with an explicit Preview marker alongside generally available capabilities such as summarization, sentiment analysis and AI coach. The capability builds custom assistance surfaces over live member conversation, so it operates on the same content as the generally available features while carrying the Pre-GA Offerings Terms: no production SLA, changeable without notice, and outside the compliance certifications the deployment relies on.
Notes: This is a specific application of this guide's baseline prohibition on Non-GA and Pre-GA features, restated because the capability appears in the same regional availability table as the generally available Agent Assist features and carries its Preview marker only in that table. Re-check the marker at the monthly release-note review; Agent Assist has moved several capabilities to general availability without a corresponding change in the feature table.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CM-7 (Least Functionality), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SA-4 (Acquisition Process)

Requirement: The CX Insights encryption specification **MUST** be initialized with a customer-managed key for every location before any conversation is ingested into that location.
Rationale: Google states plainly that you cannot change encryption key settings for a location after that location has been enabled for CMEK, and that a project already containing CX Insights data cannot be configured for customer-managed keys retroactively. This is the single most consequential irreversible decision in the suite: getting it wrong means every conversation in that location is encrypted under Google-managed keys permanently, and the only remedy is a new project.
Notes: Initialize through the InitializeEncryptionSpec API before the first ingestion, including before any proof-of-concept upload. Grant Cloud KMS CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter to `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcp-sa-ccai-cmek.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. CMEK is not available for the `global` location, which is a further reason to pin a specific region rather than accepting the default endpoint.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.312(e)(2)(ii) (Encryption); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-28(1) (Cryptographic Protection), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: A project-level `conversation_ttl` **MUST** be configured in CX Insights before the first conversation is ingested.
Rationale: Google documents that a conversation not set to expire remains in CX Insights indefinitely, and that project-level TTL only applies to conversations created after the TTL is set - changing it does not retroactively change the expiration of existing conversations. Conversations ingested during a pilot before anyone set a TTL therefore persist forever and can only be removed by locating and deleting each one individually.
Notes: Set the TTL as part of project initialization alongside the encryption specification, not as a later hardening step. Where both `expire_time` and `ttl` are set on a conversation, `expire_time` wins. Deletion occurs 24 hours after the expiration time and is not recoverable, so validate the value against the records-retention schedule before ingestion begins rather than after.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), MP-6 (Media Sanitization), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: Sensitive Data Protection redaction **MUST** be enabled on CX Insights conversation ingestion before production conversations are imported.
Rationale: CX Insights persists complete conversation transcripts and runs machine learning analysis over them, producing sentiment scores, entities, topics, and assessments that are themselves derived from the raw content. Redaction at ingestion is the control that prevents identifiers entering that corpus in the first place, and every derived artifact inherits whatever was or was not redacted at that moment.
Notes: Configure through RedactionConfig with a DLP inspect template and deidentify template. Google's ingestion documentation does not state explicitly whether redaction precedes persistence for every ingestion path, so verify with a test conversation containing synthetic identifiers and confirm they are absent from the stored transcript before enabling production ingestion.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.514(a) (De-identification of PHI); NIST 800-53: SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), SI-10 (Information Input Validation), SI-18 (Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-7 (Boundary Protection)

Requirement: Project-level `roles/contactcenterinsights.viewer` and `roles/contactcenterinsights.editor` **MUST** be granted only to a named, minimal, documented group.
Rationale: Fine-grained access control through authorized views is Pre-GA, so there is no supported way to restrict an analyst to a subset of conversations. Every holder of a project-level CX Insights role therefore sees every conversation in the project, which for a contact centre deployment is the complete corpus of member interactions rather than the sample the analyst's work requires.
Notes: Because the finer boundary does not exist in a supported form, the compensating controls are the size of the group and the visibility of its activity: keep the group small and named, review it quarterly, and rely on Data Access audit logging to record who read what. State the residual risk explicitly in the certification rather than implying a per-conversation boundary that the product does not provide.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.308(a)(4) (Information Access Management), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege), AC-2 (Account Management), AU-2 (Event Logging)

Requirement: Where authorized views are used for evaluation purposes, their filter expressions **MUST NOT** be empty.
Rationale: Google warns directly that empty filters or an empty string allow unrestricted access. An authorized view with an empty filter looks like a scoping control in the IAM policy and in any access review, while granting exactly the access it appears to constrain - a failure mode that is invisible precisely because the mechanism appears to be present.
Notes: Google also warns that granting authorized view set permissions at the project level results in users having access to all authorized view sets, which defeats the mechanism a second way. Grant on the specific view or view set, never at project level, and use the `agent_id` field for representative and team scoping. Authorized views cannot import or edit conversation data, train topic models, or create scorecards, so they do not replace the project-level roles for those tasks.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), AC-6 (Least Privilege), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)

Requirement: The CX Insights global endpoint **MUST NOT** be used for production conversation data.
Rationale: Google documents that CX Insights uses the legacy location ID `us-central1` for the global endpoint and that CMEK is not available for the `global` location. Using it therefore forfeits customer-managed encryption entirely while presenting no visible indication that it has done so, because the hostname carries no region and the default client configuration reaches it.
Notes: Both the endpoint host and the resource location path must be changed together - Google states you need to change both the host of the URL and the resource location to use the regional instance. Changing only one silently lands the data on the global instance. In Python clients this means setting the ClientOptions api_endpoint and updating the parent parameter; verify both in code review rather than in configuration documentation.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption); NIST 800-53: SA-9(5) (Processing, Storage, and Service Location), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SA-9 (External System Services)

Requirement: Cloud Storage buckets holding conversation audio for CX Insights **MUST** be encrypted with customer-managed keys, located in the approved region, and placed inside the service perimeter.
Rationale: Call audio is the richest single artifact in this suite: it carries the member's voice, everything they said before any redaction was applied, and background context that no transcript captures. It lands in a customer-owned Cloud Storage bucket whose security posture is entirely the organization's responsibility and is governed by none of the CX Insights settings.
Notes: Google documents that audio recordings cannot be written to Cloud Storage buckets outside a VPC Service Controls perimeter, so perimeter membership is a functional requirement rather than only a hardening one. Apply a lifecycle policy consistent with the conversation TTL, since the bucket has no relationship to the CX Insights expiry and will otherwise retain audio after the analysed conversation is gone.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.530(j) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-28(1) (Cryptographic Protection), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: Cloud Speech-to-Text **MUST** be configured with customer-managed encryption keys where it transcribes conversation audio for CX Insights or Agent Assist.
Rationale: Google states directly that features involving external data transfer need separate CMEK configuration in the corresponding services, naming Cloud Speech-to-Text for audio transcription. Speech-to-Text is a distinct service with its own encryption configuration, so a fully CMEK-covered CX Insights deployment still passes every second of member audio through a transcription service under Google-managed keys unless it is configured separately.
Notes: This is one of the most easily missed gaps in the suite because the transcription step is invisible in the CX Insights console - it appears as a transcript that simply exists. Include Speech-to-Text in the CMEK inventory and in the perimeter, and verify coverage by inspecting the service configuration rather than inferring it from the CX Insights encryption specification.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), SC-8 (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)

Requirement: BigQuery datasets receiving the CX Insights conversation export **MUST** be encrypted with customer-managed keys, located in the approved region, and placed inside the service perimeter.
Rationale: Google states that BigQuery needs its own CMEK configuration for conversation exports. The export is a full copy of analysed conversation content in a general-purpose analytics store governed by BigQuery IAM rather than by CX Insights roles, which means the carefully limited CX Insights access group has no bearing on who can query the exported copy.
Notes: Reconcile the BigQuery dataset's IAM against the approved CX Insights access group - a broader BigQuery grant silently widens access to the same conversation content. Apply a table expiration or partition expiration consistent with the conversation TTL, because deleting a conversation in CX Insights does not remove its exported row.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.530(j) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: Pub/Sub topics carrying CX Insights notifications **MUST NOT** be configured to convey conversation content.
Rationale: Pub/Sub notification is an event-driven integration path that routes to whatever subscribes to it, and subscribers are governed by Pub/Sub IAM rather than by any CX Insights control. A topic carrying conversation detail rather than a conversation identifier becomes an uncontrolled distribution channel for member conversation content into systems that were never assessed.
Notes: Design notifications to carry identifiers and event types so that a subscriber must call back through the authorized API path, where CX Insights IAM applies, to obtain content. Review topic and subscription IAM alongside the CX Insights access review, since a subscription created for an integration project typically outlives it. Subscriber access must additionally be restricted to approved service identities, since subscriptions are governed by Pub/Sub IAM rather than by any CX Insights control.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CA-3 (Information Exchange), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), SC-7 (Boundary Protection)

Requirement: Conversation exports to Google Sheets from CX Insights **MUST NOT** be used for conversation content.
Rationale: The Sheets integration moves analysed conversation data into a document surface governed by Workspace sharing rather than by Google Cloud IAM, where a single link change converts a controlled dataset into a broadly shared one. It also produces an uncontrolled copy that no retention setting, TTL, or deletion request in CX Insights will ever reach.
Notes: Where analysts need tabular access, direct them to the CMEK-protected BigQuery export inside the perimeter, which retains IAM control and expiration. If aggregate metrics genuinely need to reach a spreadsheet, export the aggregates rather than the conversation rows they were computed from.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI), 164.530(j) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: AC-21 (Information Sharing), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), SC-7 (Boundary Protection)

Requirement: Topic models, scorecards, summarization generators, and other artifacts trained or derived from conversation content **MUST** be treated as carrying the sensitivity of the source conversations.
Rationale: CX Insights generates a layer of derived artifacts from the conversation corpus - inferred topics, assessment results, trained topic models. These are routinely treated as aggregate analytics and shared more freely than transcripts, but they are computed from member conversation and can retain identifying detail, particularly for rare topics where a category may correspond to a single member.
Notes: Apply the same access group, retention, and residency treatment to derived artifacts as to the conversations. Pay particular attention to sparse categories: a topic matching a small number of conversations is effectively a pointer to those members. Note that authorized views cannot be used to train topic models or create scorecards, so these artifacts are produced with project-level access to the full corpus.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.514(a) (De-identification of PHI); NIST 800-53: AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), AC-21 (Information Sharing), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest)

Requirement: Where Quality AI assessments evaluate identified human representatives, their use **MUST** be approved under the organization's workforce monitoring policy before enablement.
Rationale: Quality AI produces scorecards and assessments of representative performance from conversation content, which is algorithmic evaluation of identified employees at a scale manual review never reached. That carries notice, retention, and contestability obligations distinct from the security controls protecting the conversation data itself, and assessment results are personnel data with their own access constraints.
Notes: Determine before enablement who can see individual scores, how long assessments are retained, whether they inform employment decisions, and how a representative contests one. Note that multiple scorecards remains a Preview capability, so any design depending on more than one scorecard per representative rests on a Pre-GA feature.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information), PT-5 (Privacy Notice), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: Conversations ingested into CX Insights during pilot or proof-of-concept activity **MUST** be deleted before the production deployment is certified, unless they were ingested under the full production control set.
Rationale: Pilot conversations are ingested before the controls are finished, which is the point of a pilot. If the encryption specification was not initialized, they are permanently under Google-managed keys; if no TTL was set they persist indefinitely, because the project-level TTL is not retroactive; and if redaction was not configured they hold unredacted member content that every subsequent analysis inherits.
Notes: Enumerate and delete pilot conversations explicitly rather than assuming a later TTL will collect them - Google is explicit that changing the TTL does not retroactively change the expiration of existing conversations. Where the encryption specification was not set correctly at pilot time, deleting the conversations does not fix the location, and a new project is the remedy.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: MP-6 (Media Sanitization), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest)

Requirement: CX Agent Studio **MUST** be CMEK-integrated at project creation, before any agent application or conversation data exists in the project.
Rationale: Google states that existing resources in non-CMEK integrated projects cannot be CMEK integrated retroactively. A project that begins without CMEK therefore holds agent instructions, tool configurations, application variables, and conversation history under Google-managed keys permanently, and the only remedy is a new project with everything rebuilt in it.
Notes: Treat CMEK integration as a project provisioning step in the same class as enabling the API, not as a hardening task. Google notes that one key should be used per project location. Verify integration by reading the configuration back before the first agent application is created, because the failure is silent and only discovered when someone later asks whether the project is covered.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.312(e)(2)(ii) (Encryption); NIST 800-53: SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SC-28(1) (Cryptographic Protection), SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: Cloud KMS keys protecting Gemini Enterprise for CX data **MUST** be monitored for availability, with key destruction and disablement gated on multi-party authorization.
Rationale: Google warns that if a key is revoked for more than 30 days, the CX Insights data encrypted by that key will be lost. This converts an ordinary key management error - a mistaken disable, an over-eager cleanup of an apparently unused key, an expired rotation schedule - into permanent destruction of the member conversation corpus on a 30-day fuse, with no recovery path once it burns.
Notes: Alert on key state changes and on decryption failures against these keys, and treat any such alert as an availability incident with a hard 30-day clock rather than a configuration ticket. Protect key destruction with organization policy and a separate approval, and confirm the KMS key's own IAM excludes the people who administer the CX projects.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption), 164.308(a)(7) (Contingency Plan); NIST 800-53: SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), CP-9 (System Backup), AC-5 (Separation of Duties), SI-4 (System Monitoring)

Requirement: Key rotation schedules for Gemini Enterprise for CX **MUST** account for the vendor's statement that data re-encryption is not performed on rotation.
Rationale: Google states that key rotation is supported but data re-encryption is not. Rotation therefore protects only newly written data, and previously written conversation content stays bound to the older key version indefinitely. A rotation policy that assumes the whole corpus moves forward - and that consequently retires old key versions on a schedule - will destroy data it believes it has already migrated.
Notes: Retain every key version for as long as any data encrypted under it is retained, which means key version lifetime is governed by the conversation retention schedule rather than by the rotation period. Document this explicitly, because it contradicts the default assumption behind most rotation standards.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) (Encryption and Decryption); NIST 800-53: SC-12 (Cryptographic Key Establishment and Management), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: CX Agent Studio agent data **MUST** be located in the `us` multi-region.
Rationale: CX Agent Studio offers exactly two multi-regions, `us` and `eu`, and the region governs where callback code, tool code and configurations, agent instructions and prompts, application variables, and conversation history are stored at rest. Member conversation content for a US population belongs in the US multi-region both to satisfy the organization's residency position and to keep the data path within a single legal jurisdiction.
Notes: A region must be supplied on every API request through the location path or resource parameter, so an omitted or defaulted region in client code is a residency defect that no console setting reveals. Verify the region in deployed client configuration rather than in design documentation.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SA-9(5) (Processing, Storage, and Service Location), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SA-9 (External System Services)

Requirement: Cloud Logging **MUST** be configured with a US region for log storage independently of the Gemini Enterprise for CX residency setting.
Rationale: Google's residency documentation for CX Agent Studio directs the reader to the Cloud Logging documentation to control where logs are stored, which means logging sits outside the product's residency guarantee. Because conversation data is documented as landing in Cloud Logging as one of the customer-owned storage paths, an unpinned logging configuration relocates member conversation content outside the residency boundary the rest of the deployment maintains.
Notes: Pin the log bucket region explicitly for every project in the deployment, and confirm that any log sink forwarding to a SIEM does not itself relocate the data. This is a separate configuration in a separate product, so it is routinely missed in a residency review that only examines the CX components.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SA-9(5) (Processing, Storage, and Service Location), AU-4 (Audit Log Storage Capacity), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SA-9 (External System Services)

Requirement: Conversation history retention in CX Agent Studio **MUST** be configured to a documented period no longer than the business need requires.
Rationale: Google documents retention as configurable with a default of one year and a maximum of two. Left at the default, the deployment accumulates a year of complete member conversation history because nobody made a decision, and the volume of that corpus is the primary determinant of the impact of any future compromise of the analytics surface.
Notes: Set the value against the records-retention schedule and the operational need for dispute resolution, and record the rationale. Note that this setting governs the CX Agent Studio conversation store only - the CX Insights corpus, the Cloud Storage audio, the BigQuery export, and Cloud Logging each expire on their own schedules and must be aligned deliberately. Leaving the setting at its one-year default is not a decision.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), MP-6 (Media Sanitization), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention)

Requirement: The state of the Log your customer conversations setting **MUST** be an explicit, documented decision for every agent application.
Rationale: This single toggle governs whether long-term conversational data exists at all: Google states that disabling it disables all types of long-term conversational data except BigQuery data, and that with logging disabled conversational data does not exist in any Google-owned persistent storage to be accessed. It is simultaneously the strongest available data minimization control and a control that disables the monitoring dashboards and the CX Insights corpus that operations depends on.
Notes: Because the trade is real, make it deliberately rather than by default. Note the exception in Google's own wording - BigQuery data is not disabled by the toggle - so a deployment that turns logging off while an export remains configured has not stopped conversation content being persisted. Record the decision and the exception check as certification evidence.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.530(j) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), AU-2 (Event Logging), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement)

Requirement: Google's contractual position on the use of Gemini Enterprise for CX conversation content for model training **MUST** be confirmed in writing and retained as certification evidence.
Rationale: The conversation history documentation states that Google enforces a strict policy that customer content shared using this toggle is never used to train Google's production machine learning models. That statement is scoped to one toggle on one page of one component, and this suite has four components with several distinct data paths, including audio through Speech-to-Text and analytics in CX Insights.
Notes: Obtain the position through the contracting relationship covering all four components and every data path, rather than relying on a documentation sentence that Google can revise without notice. Retain the response as evidence, and re-confirm at contract renewal and whenever a new component is enabled.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI), 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.504(e) (Business Associate Contracts); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information), CA-3 (Information Exchange)

Requirement: Sensitive Data Protection templates used by any Gemini Enterprise for CX component **MUST** be located inside the same VPC Service Controls perimeter as the component that references them.
Rationale: Google states that Sensitive Data Protection redaction templates outside the perimeter cause failures in redacting conversation contents. The failure mode matters more than the failure: redaction stops working while ingestion continues, so unredacted member content flows into the conversation corpus and the misconfiguration surfaces as a data problem discovered later rather than as an error at the time.
Notes: Verify template location as part of perimeter change review, and monitor for redaction failures as an operational signal rather than assuming success. Because a template can be moved or a perimeter redrawn independently of the CX configuration, re-verify after any change to either.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.514(a) (De-identification of PHI); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SI-18 (Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: Member identifiers and other sensitive values **MUST NOT** be written into application variables, agent instructions, or tool configuration as static values.
Rationale: Application variables and agent instructions are documented as agent data at rest, readable by every holder of the viewer role and carried in configuration exports. A member identifier placed there persists beyond the conversation that produced it, is not covered by conversation retention or TTL settings, and is not subject to the redaction applied to conversation content.
Notes: Use dynamic variables populated per session for values that vary by member, so the value lives with the session rather than with the configuration. Include a scan for identifier-shaped values in the pre-deployment agent review, alongside the credential scan.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest), SI-18 (Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations)

Requirement: A documented procedure **MUST** exist to locate and delete all copies of an individual member's conversation data across every store in the deployment.
Rationale: Conversation content is written to at least six places: the Google-managed CX Agent Studio store, CX Insights, Cloud Storage audio, Cloud Logging, the BigQuery export, and any Pub/Sub subscriber. Each has its own deletion mechanism and its own retention clock, and deleting a conversation in one does not remove it from the others. A deletion obligation the organization cannot execute completely is a compliance failure regardless of intent.
Notes: Build the procedure against the store inventory rather than against the console, and test it end to end with a synthetic conversation, verifying absence in every store afterwards. CX Agent Studio provides a DeleteConversation operation and CX Insights supports individual deletion; the BigQuery export and Cloud Storage audio require their own steps.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.526 (Amendment of PHI), 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.502(b) (Minimum Necessary); NIST 800-53: SI-12 (Information Management and Retention), MP-6 (Media Sanitization), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), CM-8 (System Component Inventory)

Requirement: The short-lived caches the product maintains **SHOULD** be documented in the data flow record supporting certification.
Rationale: Google documents a session memcache holding active session management data and metadata with a 30-minute TTL, and a Text-to-Speech Memstore cache with a one-hour TTL. These are minor exposures individually, but an incomplete data flow diagram is a finding in its own right, and an assessor who discovers an undocumented store asks what else was omitted.
Notes: Record them as transient stores with their stated TTLs rather than attempting to control them - the product exposes no configuration for either. Their presence is also the reason a deletion request cannot be confirmed complete within the first hour of a conversation ending.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures), CM-8 (System Component Inventory), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: Where Google support access to Google-managed conversation data is a concern for the deployment, that access **SHOULD** be monitored through Access Transparency.
Rationale: Google documents that support may access Google-managed operational data for critical debugging and system maintenance. For a corpus of member conversation content this is provider access to ePHI, and it is permitted under the business associate relationship, so the control available is not prevention but a record of when it occurred.
Notes: Enable Access Transparency where the organization's licensing supports it and route the logs to the same destination as the audit logs. Confirm which services in this suite are within Access Transparency's coverage rather than assuming the whole deployment is, since coverage is enumerated per service and changes over time.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review), 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts); NIST 800-53: AU-2 (Event Logging), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), SA-9 (External System Services), SI-4 (System Monitoring)

Requirement: A VPC Service Controls perimeter **MUST** be configured with both `ces.googleapis.com` and `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com` in the restricted services list.
Rationale: These two API services are the entire data plane of the suite: `ces.googleapis.com` carries agent configuration, tool invocation, and live conversation, and `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com` carries the analysed conversation corpus. Restricting only one leaves the other reachable with stolen credentials from any network, which for the Insights service means the complete member conversation corpus.
Notes: Google names both services explicitly in its perimeter guidance for this product. Add the supporting services in the data path to the same perimeter - Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, Speech-to-Text, and Sensitive Data Protection - because each is a documented breakage point when left outside.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: The service perimeter **MUST** be established and enforced before agent applications, data stores, deployment channels, and CX Insights locations are created.
Rationale: Google documents seven distinct operations that fail once a perimeter is enforced around existing resources: tools and callbacks reaching arbitrary HTTP endpoints, Cloud Storage audio writes, BigQuery export, Sensitive Data Protection redaction templates, OpenAPI tool secrets, data store tool execution, and cross-perimeter agent references and import or export. Enforcing a perimeter after the fact therefore produces a wave of simultaneous production failures at exactly the moment there is pressure to write exceptions rather than relocate resources.
Notes: The vendor documentation does not itself state a sequencing requirement - this control is derived from the enumerated breakages rather than quoted from Google. Sequence as: define the perimeter, add restricted services, configure ingress and egress rules, validate in dry-run, enforce, then create resources. Every exception written under production pressure is a permanent hole that nobody revisits.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures), CM-4 (Impact Analyses)

Requirement: The service perimeter **MUST** be validated in dry-run mode and its findings resolved before enforcement.
Rationale: Dry-run mode reports what enforcement would block without blocking it, which is the only safe way to discover which of the seven documented breakage paths a given deployment actually depends on. Skipping it means discovering the same information as a production outage, and outage-driven remediation reliably produces broad exceptions instead of relocated resources.
Notes: Run the dry-run across a full operational cycle rather than a single test conversation, because several breakage paths - BigQuery export, audio writes, redaction template access - only occur on batch or asynchronous operations. Resolve each finding by moving the resource inside the perimeter, not by exempting the service.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CA-2 (Control Assessments), CM-4 (Impact Analyses)

Requirement: Tools and callbacks **MUST NOT** be configured to send requests to arbitrary public HTTP endpoints.
Rationale: Google states that tools and callbacks are not able to send requests to arbitrary HTTP endpoints when VPC Service Controls is enabled without Service Directory configuration. Outside a perimeter this is the primary uncontrolled egress path in the product: a tool URL is an outbound channel for conversation-derived parameters, configurable by any holder of the tools editor role, reaching any host on the internet.
Notes: Maintain an approved list of tool target endpoints as part of the tool inventory and reconcile it on the quarterly review. Configure Service Directory private network access for targets inside the organization's VPC so that the supported path exists before the perimeter makes it mandatory.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CA-3 (Information Exchange)

Requirement: Service Directory private network access **MUST** be configured for OpenAPI tool targets hosted inside the organization's VPC network.
Rationale: Google documents Service Directory integration as the supported path that keeps traffic within the Google Cloud network and enforces IAM and VPC Service Controls for OpenAPI tool targets. It is the only mechanism that lets a tool reach an internal system without either exposing that system publicly or breaking under perimeter enforcement.
Notes: Grant `servicedirectory.viewer` and `servicedirectory.pscAuthorizedService` to `service-agent-project-number@gcp-sa-ces.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and where Service Directory resides in a different project grant `servicedirectory.viewer` in both projects. Configure this before perimeter enforcement so tool connectivity is already on the supported path.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), SC-8 (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity), CA-9 (Internal System Connections)

Requirement: Cloud Storage buckets, BigQuery datasets, Secret Manager secrets, Sensitive Data Protection templates, and data stores referenced by Gemini Enterprise for CX **MUST** reside inside the same service perimeter as the components that reference them.
Rationale: Google enumerates each of these as a specific failure: audio recordings cannot be written to buckets outside the perimeter, conversation data cannot be written to external BigQuery datasets, OpenAPI tools cannot reference secrets outside the perimeter, external redaction templates cause redaction failures, and data store tools specifying a data store outside the perimeter fail to execute. A resource outside the perimeter is therefore both a security gap and a functional break.
Notes: Enumerate every referenced resource before enforcement, because these references are created by different roles at different times and no single console view lists them together. The redaction template case is the most dangerous of the five, since it degrades data protection rather than producing an obvious failure.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(e)(1) (Transmission Security), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), SC-7(10) (Prevent Exfiltration)

Requirement: Perimeter ingress and egress rules **MUST** be deny by default, with each exception documented, owned, and reviewed at least annually.
Rationale: A perimeter's value is determined entirely by its exception list, and exceptions accumulate under delivery pressure - most often during the enforcement cutover, when a broad rule restores service faster than relocating a resource. An unreviewed exception list converts the perimeter into documentation rather than a control.
Notes: Record for each exception what it permits, who requested it, and what would have to change for it to be removed. Exceptions added during a cutover deserve particular scrutiny because they were written to end an outage rather than to express an authorization decision.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), SC-7(5) (Deny by Default - Allow by Exception), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

Requirement: Flow-based agents **MUST NOT** reference agent resources located outside the service perimeter.
Rationale: Google documents that flow-based agents referencing external agent resources fail under perimeter enforcement. Beyond the functional break, a cross-perimeter agent reference is a delegation across a security boundary in which the invoked agent executes with its own project's service agent permissions, so the reference silently extends reach into a project the calling perimeter does not govern.
Notes: Keep the full agent delegation graph inside a single perimeter and review it whenever a new agent reference is added. A reference that crosses perimeters should be treated as a design finding rather than a configuration option.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AC-3 (Access Enforcement), CA-3 (Information Exchange)

Requirement: Import and export operations for agent configuration **MUST** target Cloud Storage buckets inside the service perimeter.
Rationale: Google documents that import and export operations targeting external Cloud Storage buckets fail under perimeter enforcement. Export carries the complete agent configuration - instructions, tool definitions, and application variables - so an export to a bucket outside the perimeter is a full disclosure of the deployment's logic and its integration topology.
Notes: Restrict the export destinations to a small set of perimeter-internal buckets under change control, and treat an export as a sensitive operation in its own right since Admin Activity audit logs record import and export.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AC-4 (Information Flow Enforcement), AU-2 (Event Logging), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

Requirement: Changes to the service perimeter protecting Gemini Enterprise for CX **MUST** be change controlled and alerted on.
Rationale: The perimeter is the compensating control for several exposures this product cannot address internally, including the service-agent tool execution model and the absence of supported per-conversation scoping in the analytics surface. Because a single policy edit can remove a service from the restricted list without any visible effect on the application, perimeter changes are both high impact and low friction.
Notes: Alert on Access Context Manager policy changes and route them to the security operations queue rather than to the platform team that made them. Reconcile the restricted service list against the documented baseline on the quarterly configuration review.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), SI-4 (System Monitoring)

Requirement: Data Access audit logs **MUST** be explicitly enabled for `ces.googleapis.com`.
Rationale: Google documents that Admin Activity audit logs are enabled by default while Data Access logs require explicit enablement. For CX Agent Studio the Data Access tier is the one that records agent and tool operations and conversation deletion - the reads and writes touching member conversation content. Without it, the audit trail covers who created an application but not who used it or what it reached.
Notes: Enable at organization level so new projects inherit the configuration rather than depending on a project-creation checklist. Verify with a filter on `protoPayload.serviceName="ces.googleapis.com"` after enablement, and note that long-running operations produce two entries, one at start and one at completion.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review); NIST 800-53: AU-2 (Event Logging), AU-12 (Audit Record Generation), AU-3 (Content of Audit Records), CM-6 (Configuration Settings)

Requirement: Data Access audit logs **MUST** be explicitly enabled for `contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com`.
Rationale: CX Insights holds the complete analysed conversation corpus and, because fine-grained access control is Pre-GA, every approved user can read all of it. The Data Access log is therefore the only record of which analyst read which member's conversation, which makes it the primary compensating control for the absence of a supported per-conversation access boundary.
Notes: The DATA_READ tier covers conversation analysis, model management, rule creation, feedback labeling, and assessment operations. Verify with a filter on `protoPayload.serviceName="contactcenterinsights.googleapis.com"`. Given the breadth of standing access, retention and reviewability of these logs matter more here than anywhere else in the deployment.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review), 164.312(a)(1) (Access Control); NIST 800-53: AU-2 (Event Logging), AU-12 (Audit Record Generation), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), AC-3 (Access Enforcement)

Requirement: Audit logs from every Gemini Enterprise for CX project **MUST** be exported to the organization's security information and event management platform.
Rationale: Cloud Logging retention is bounded and project-scoped, and detection of misuse across a multi-project deployment requires correlation that a per-project log view cannot provide. Exporting is also what places the records outside the control of the same administrators whose actions they record.
Notes: Export Admin Activity, Data Access, and any Access Transparency logs through an aggregated sink at organization or folder level so a newly created project is covered without action. Confirm that the sink destination does not relocate the data outside the residency boundary maintained elsewhere in the deployment.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review); NIST 800-53: AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information), SI-4 (System Monitoring), AU-4 (Audit Log Storage Capacity)

Requirement: Audit log retention **MUST** meet or exceed the organization's retention requirement for records of access to protected health information.
Rationale: Data Access logs for these services are the evidence of who read member conversation content, and their value in an investigation or a breach determination is a direct function of how far back they reach. Cloud Logging's default retention is shorter than the retention obligation that applies to records of PHI access.
Notes: The regulatory floor is six years: HIPAA 164.316(b)(2) requires documentation, including records of access to protected health information, to be retained for six years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later. Cloud Logging's default bucket retention is far shorter. Set retention on the log bucket or the export destination rather than relying on defaults, and confirm the destination is immutable or write-once for the retention period. Retention on the exported copy is what matters if the project itself is compromised or deleted.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.530(j) (Documentation), 164.316(b)(2) (Time Limit); NIST 800-53: AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), AU-4 (Audit Log Storage Capacity), AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: Exported audit logs **MUST** be protected against modification and deletion by the administrators of the Gemini Enterprise for CX projects.
Rationale: The administrators of these projects are the population whose actions the logs record. Where the same identities can edit sinks, alter retention, or delete log buckets, the audit trail attests only to activity that the administrator chose to leave in place, which is not an audit trail.
Notes: Route the export to a project under separate administrative control with its own IAM, and restrict log bucket and sink modification to the logging or security function. Alert on changes to sink configuration and log retention as security events.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.312(c)(1) (Integrity); NIST 800-53: AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information), AU-9(4) (Access by Subset of Privileged Users), AC-5 (Separation of Duties), AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Requirement: Alerts **MUST** be configured for changes to CX Agent Studio security settings.
Rationale: Security settings are project-wide and govern redaction, retention, and export behaviour, so a single change there alters the data protection posture of every agent in the project at once. The change requires only the security settings editor role, produces no deployment, and is invisible to anyone reading an individual agent's configuration.
Notes: Alert on the security settings update operations recorded in Admin Activity logs under `ces.googleapis.com` and route to the security operations queue. Correlate each alert with an approved change record; an unmatched change is the highest-value single signal available in this deployment.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review); NIST 800-53: SI-4 (System Monitoring), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), IR-4 (Incident Handling)

Requirement: Alerts **MUST** be configured for conversation deletion and bulk deletion operations in CX Agent Studio and CX Insights.
Rationale: Conversation deletion is both a legitimate privacy operation and the natural final step of an attacker or an insider covering their activity. CX Insights supports bulk operations over conversations, which makes large-scale destruction a single API call, and expiry-based deletion is documented as not recoverable.
Notes: Alert on DeleteConversation and the bulk delete operations in both services, and distinguish deletions performed through the documented privacy procedure from ad hoc ones. A deletion volume anomaly is worth investigating even where each individual deletion appears authorized.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.312(b) (Audit Controls), 164.312(c)(1) (Integrity), 164.308(a)(6) (Security Incident Procedures); NIST 800-53: SI-4 (System Monitoring), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), IR-4 (Incident Handling), AU-2 (Event Logging)

Requirement: Alerts **SHOULD** be configured for tool registration and modification in CX Agent Studio.
Rationale: A new tool immediately extends what every agent in the project can reach, because tools execute with the project service agent's permissions. Tool registration is therefore a change to the deployment's effective authorization boundary made by a single role holder with no deployment step and no approval gate in the product.
Notes: Alert on tool create and update operations in Data Access logs under `ces.googleapis.com` and reconcile against the tool inventory. A registration with no corresponding inventory entry is either an undocumented integration or a compromise, and both warrant the same first question.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-4 (System Monitoring), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), CM-8 (System Component Inventory), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting)

Requirement: Alerts **SHOULD** be configured for anomalous read volume against CX Insights conversation data.
Rationale: Because every approved CX Insights user can read every conversation, the difference between legitimate analysis and bulk extraction is volume and pattern rather than authorization. No preventive control distinguishes them, so detection is the available control and it depends entirely on the Data Access log being both enabled and monitored.
Notes: Baseline normal analyst read volume before setting thresholds, and alert on deviation rather than on an absolute count, since legitimate quality review is itself high volume. Pair with the quarterly entitlement review so that an unexpected reader is noticed as well as an unexpected volume.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) (Information System Activity Review), 164.312(b) (Audit Controls); NIST 800-53: SI-4 (System Monitoring), AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting), AC-6(7) (Review of User Privileges), IR-4 (Incident Handling), AC-6 (Least Privilege)

Requirement: Operational monitoring **MUST NOT** depend solely on the product's built-in conversation dashboards where conversation logging is disabled or can be disabled.
Rationale: Google notes that disabling the conversation logging toggle affects the monitoring dashboards, which couples the data minimization decision to the observability capability. A monitoring practice that assumes those dashboards will be populated becomes silently blind if the toggle is turned off for a privacy reason on a different team's initiative.
Notes: Base operational and security monitoring on audit logs and platform metrics, which are unaffected by the toggle, and treat the product dashboards as a convenience layer. Record the dependency so the observability consequence is visible to whoever considers changing the logging setting.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: SI-4 (System Monitoring), AU-2 (Event Logging), CM-6 (Configuration Settings), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

Requirement: An incident response procedure covering Gemini Enterprise for CX **MUST** be documented, including containment steps for a compromised agent application or tool.
Rationale: The containment actions in this product are specific and not obvious under pressure: rolling back an agent version, revoking the query-access client role from a channel, removing a tool registration, disabling a deployment, and tightening the perimeter. A generic cloud incident procedure will not name any of them, and a live agent continues serving members throughout the delay.
Notes: Document who can execute each containment action and confirm they can reach it outside business hours. Exercise the agent version rollback at least once before relying on it. Where an incident involves member conversation content, the breach determination path and the notification clock apply as they would to any other ePHI disclosure.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(6) (Security Incident Procedures), 164.404 (Notification to Individuals), 164.410 (Notification by a Business Associate), 164.408 (Notification to the Secretary); NIST 800-53: IR-4 (Incident Handling), IR-6 (Incident Reporting), CP-9 (System Backup), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)

Requirement: A business associate agreement covering Google Cloud **MUST** be executed and its scope confirmed to include every Gemini Enterprise for CX component in use before production member conversation data is processed.
Rationale: Every component of this suite processes protected health information in its most unstructured and least controllable form. Google's BAA covers the infrastructure and the services named in the covered products list, and coverage attaches per product rather than per platform, so an executed BAA is a necessary but not sufficient condition and its scope must be checked against the specific components deployed.
Notes: Confirm coverage before enablement rather than at annual review, since the components are enabled independently and by different teams. Retain the confirmation as certification evidence with the date it was checked, because the covered products list is revised as products are added.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.314(a) (Business Associate Contracts or Other Arrangements), 164.502(e) (Disclosures to Business Associates); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), CA-3 (Information Exchange)

Requirement: Only Gemini Enterprise for CX components named in Google's HIPAA covered products list **MUST** be used to process protected health information.
Rationale: Google's covered products list names individually, and verbatim, Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience (GECX), Customer Experience Agent Studio, CX Insights, Contact Center AI Agent Assist, and Conversational Agents. A component absent from that list is outside the BAA regardless of being reachable from the same console and billed on the same invoice, and processing ePHI through it is an unauthorized disclosure.
Notes: Check the list per component before enablement and again at each annual reassessment. Note that Commerce agents does not appear in the list at the time of authoring, which is a second and independent reason it must not be deployed alongside its unreleased status.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.502(e) (Disclosures to Business Associates), 164.502(a) (Uses and Disclosures of PHI); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), CM-7 (Least Functionality), SA-4 (Acquisition Process), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: Google Cloud surfaces branded Dialogflow **MUST NOT** be used to process protected health information within this deployment.
Rationale: Dialogflow by that name is not present in Google's HIPAA covered products list, while Conversational Agents is. Because CX Agent Studio is documented as an evolution of Dialogflow CX and CX Insights accepts ingestion from Dialogflow, a deployment can reach a Dialogflow-branded surface through a supported integration path and leave BAA coverage without any deliberate decision.
Notes: Audit the ingestion configuration specifically: CX Insights lists Dialogflow among its integration sources, so a legacy contact centre integration may be routing conversations through it. Where a Dialogflow-branded resource is in the path, confirm with Google which covered product name applies to it before treating it as in scope.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts), 164.502(e) (Disclosures to Business Associates); NIST 800-53: SA-9 (External System Services), CM-8 (System Component Inventory), CM-7 (Least Functionality), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: Compliance attestations relied upon for Gemini Enterprise for CX **MUST** be retrieved, reviewed, and their exclusions tracked at least annually.
Rationale: An attestation is a point-in-time statement with a defined scope, and the useful information is usually in what it excludes rather than what it covers. For a suite whose components are certified individually and whose supporting services - Speech-to-Text, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud KMS, Pub/Sub - carry their own scope, the compliance picture is a composition rather than a single document.
Notes: Track the exclusions as a register rather than filing the reports. An exclusion that overlaps a control this guide depends on is a finding to escalate, not a footnote, and it will not announce itself between annual reviews.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation), 164.308(b)(1) (Business Associate Contracts); NIST 800-53: CA-2 (Control Assessments), SA-9 (External System Services), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

Requirement: The complete data flow for member conversation content across all Gemini Enterprise for CX components and supporting services **MUST** be documented and maintained as certification evidence.
Rationale: Conversation content is written to at least six stores across two product APIs and five supporting Google Cloud services, each with independent encryption, residency, retention, and access configuration. Without a maintained data flow record, no one can answer where a given member's conversation exists, and every deletion, residency, and breach-scope question becomes an investigation.
Notes: The record must name each store, the service that owns it, its encryption configuration, its region, its retention clock, and who can read it. Refresh it whenever a component, ingestion source, export, or subscriber is added, since each of those creates a new copy rather than a new view.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (Risk Analysis), 164.316(b)(1) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures), CM-8 (System Component Inventory), RA-3 (Risk Assessment), SI-12 (Information Management and Retention)

Requirement: The residual risks this product cannot mitigate **MUST** be documented and formally accepted before production certification.
Rationale: Three exposures in this suite have no configuration remedy: tools execute with the project service agent's permissions rather than the caller's, data store retrieval is not documented as permission-aware, and per-conversation scoping in the analytics surface is available only as a Pre-GA feature. Each is compensated in this guide rather than closed, and a certification that does not name them implies a boundary that does not exist.
Notes: State each residual risk with the compensating control that bounds it and the accepting authority. This is the record a later reviewer needs in order to distinguish a control that was considered and bounded from one that was overlooked.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A) (Risk Analysis), 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B) (Risk Management), 164.316(b)(1) (Documentation); NIST 800-53: RA-3 (Risk Assessment), CA-2 (Control Assessments), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures), SA-8 (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles); NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1): GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE

Requirement: Gemini Enterprise for CX agent applications **MUST** be registered in the organization's AI system inventory with a named accountable owner.
Rationale: A member-facing generative agent making statements about coverage and benefits is a consequential AI system under every governance framework the organization is likely to be measured against, and this suite makes creating one a low-friction action available to any holder of an editor role. An inventory is what makes the population of deployed agents knowable to the people accountable for them.
Notes: Register the agent, its purpose, its audience, its tool reach, and its accountable owner, and reconcile the inventory against the deployed agents on the quarterly cycle. The reconciliation is the control - an unregistered production agent is the finding it exists to surface.
Mappings: NIST 800-53: CM-8 (System Component Inventory), PL-8 (Security and Privacy Architectures), RA-3 (Risk Assessment), PT-2 (Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information); NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1): GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE

Requirement: The security posture of this deployment **MUST** be reassessed whenever a Gemini Enterprise for CX component transitions a capability from Preview to general availability.
Rationale: Several controls in this guide exist because a capability is Pre-GA, most consequentially the compensating access model that stands in for CX Insights fine-grained access control. When such a capability reaches GA the compensating control becomes unnecessary overhead and the stronger native control becomes available, so a guide that is never revisited keeps the organization on the weaker posture indefinitely.
Notes: The monthly release-note review is the trigger. On a Preview-to-GA transition, revisit the requirement that prohibited the capability, the compensating control that stood in for it, and the residual risk that was accepted because of it - all three change together. Increment the Revision column on each affected row rather than renumbering.
Mappings: HIPAA: 164.308(a)(8) (Evaluation); NIST 800-53: CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring), CM-3 (Configuration Change Control), RA-3 (Risk Assessment), CA-2 (Control Assessments); NIST AI RMF (AI 100-1): GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE
